claims.text: On the last day of the feast of Double Mirth, Melko went to Sirnúmen, where many of the Gnomes lived at that time, and killed those guarding the treasures; then he proceeded to kill Bruithwir and seized their most glorious jewels, including the Silmarils.
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), The Book of Lost Tales Part One, "VI. The Theft of Melko and the Darkening of Valinor", p. 145

claims.text: His tomb was known as the Mound of the First Sorrow, which was so named because of all the sorrow that Bruithwir's death caused afterwards.
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), The Book of Lost Tales Part One, "VI. The Theft of Melko and the Darkening of Valinor", pp. 149-50

claims.text: Bruno was the son of Blanco and Primrose. He had a younger sister, the infamous Lobelia Sackville-Baggins, and two children, Hugo and Hilda.
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, The Lord of the Rings, Appendix C, "Boffin of the Yale"

claims.text: Bruno attended Bilbo's Farewell Party.
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, The Lord of the Rings, Appendix C, "Boffin of the Yale"

claims.text: Brytta was the son of Fréaláf Hildeson and the grandnephew of king Helm of Rohan. He was the grandson of the King's sister Hild.
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, The Lord of the Rings, Appendix A, "The House of Eorl", entry for king Helm Hammerhand, pp. 1066-7

claims.text: During the reign of Helm, when Brytta was still a child, Rohan was invaded by the Dunlendings in and conquered the capital of Edoras. The survivors were enslaved and others fled to the valleys of the White Mountains. Brytta's father, Fréaláf, fled with many others to the mountain refuge at Dunharrow. King Helm retreated with his surviving forces to the Hornburg and was besieged by the invaders.
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, The Lord of the Rings, Appendix A, "The House of Eorl", entry for king Helm Hammerhand, pp. 1066-7

claims.text: A short time afterwards the Long Winter came and covered Rohan in snow. The cold and famine that followed caused great suffering for both the Rohirrim and the invaders, and King Helm with his sons lost their lives. Soon after the end of the winter, Fréalaf led a small company from Dunharrow, liberated Edoras by surprise and killed the Dunlending leader Wulf. Before the end of the Dunlendings were driven from Rohan.
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, The Lord of the Rings, Appendix A, "The House of Eorl", entry for king Helm Hammerhand, pp. 1066-7

claims.text: Fréaláf was crowned as the new King of Rohan. The wizard Saruman came to the crowning bringing gifts and took up residence in the Gondorian fortress of Isengard, with the permission of Steward Beren of Gondor.
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, The Lord of the Rings, Appendix A, "The House of Eorl", entry for king Fréaláf, p. 1068

claims.text: Brytta became king after the death of his father in .
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, The Lord of the Rings, Appendix A, "The House of Eorl", "The Kings of the Mark", Second Line, entry 2726-2798 10. Fréaláf Hildeson, p. 1068

claims.text: During his reign Rohan was still recovering from the war with the Dunlendings during which many Rohirrim had died and many of their cattle and horses had been lost. Brytta was generous and helped those in need. His people called him Léofa, because he was loved by all.
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, The Lord of the Rings, Appendix A, "The House of Eorl", entry for king Fréaláf, p. 1068; J.R.R. Tolkien, The Lord of the Rings, Appendix A, "The House of Eorl", "The Kings of the Mark", Second Line, entry 2752-2842 11. Brytta, p. 1068

claims.text: His rule saw a new trouble, as the final battle of the War of the Dwarves and Orcs caused great numbers of Orcs to flee from the Misty Mountains, trying to make a home in the White Mountains in the south of Rohan. During his rule the Rohirrim hunted down the Orcs.
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, The Lord of the Rings, Appendix A, "The Númenorean Kings", "Gondor and the Heirs of Anárion", "The Stewards", entry for steward Beregond, p. 1054; J.R.R. Tolkien, The Lord of the Rings, Appendix A, "The House of Eorl", "The Kings of the Mark", Second Line, entry 2752-2842 11. Brytta, p. 1068

claims.text: Brytta was the longest-lived king of the Second Line (from Fréaláf to Théoden) and ruled for 44 years until his death in 2842, at which it was believed that Rohan was free of the Orcs. He was buried in the second mound on the east-side of the Barrow-field, on the left side of the road that approached Edoras from the north-west.
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, The Lord of the Rings, Appendix A, "The House of Eorl", "The Kings of the Mark", pp. 1068-9; J.R.R. Tolkien, The Lord of the Rings, Appendix A, "The House of Eorl", "The Kings of the Mark", Second Line, entry 2752-2842 11. Brytta, p. 1068; J.R.R. Tolkien, The Lord of the Rings, The Return of the King, "Many Partings", p. 977; J.R.R. Tolkien, The Lord of the Rings, The Two Towers, "The King of the Golden Hall", p. 507; J.R.R. Tolkien, The Lord of the Rings, The Return of the King, "Map of Rohan, Gondor, and Mordor"

claims.text: Brytta was succeeded by his son Walda at his death.
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, The Lord of the Rings, Appendix A, "The House of Eorl", "The Kings of the Mark", Second Line, entry 2780-2851 12. Walda, p. 1069

claims.text: In the first edition of The Lord of the Rings Léofa was called Léof and there was no note about the events during his life in his entry in the list of Kings of the Mark.
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), The Peoples of Middle-earth, "IX. The Making of Appendix A": (iii) "The House of Eorl", Notes, note 5

The word Bucca is Old English for "buck", "male deer" or "he-goat" which is a translation of the original Westron name Gamba.

claims.text: Around , some four years after the fall of the North-kingdom, the Hobbits of the Shire elected from their midst one Bucca of the Marish as the first Thain. He was to rule the land in the King's stead. Little else is known about him, other than that he brought peace and prosperity to the Hobbits.
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, The Lord of the Rings, Appendix B, "The Third Age"
claims.finding_aid: Tolkien Gateway, “Bucca of the Marish”, revid 395854 (2024-06-25T19:11:36Z)

claims.text: Buffo Boffin of the Yale married Ivy Goodenough, and had four children: Bosco, Basso, Briffo, and Berylla.
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, The Lord of the Rings, Appendix C, "Boffin of the Yale"

claims.text: During his days of youth, Buldar fought in the army of the North King in the valley of Ishmalog against the "Fell Folk" and came back home to Agar with "a wound, a sword and a woman". The latter, named Elmar, he wedded mostly against her wish and had many sons, of which the youngest was Hazad. Elmar warned Buldar, however,that though ehe was forced to live with him she would have her vengeance: one of her bloodline would arise in Agar and bring about the downfall of Buldar's folk.
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), The Peoples of Middle-earth, "XVII. Tal-Elmar"

claims.text:
In a penciled note added to the manuscripts, J.R.R. Tolkien proposed that Buldar should be left out of the story and Elmar to be Hazad's wife. However, in the published version, this change did not occur.
The rejected version of Buldar’s name is Tal-Bulda.
Category:Second Age characters
Category:People of Agar
Category:Mannish words
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), The Peoples of Middle-earth, "XVII. Tal-Elmar", note 5

claims.text: The name Bungo was meaningless in contemporary Hobbitish Westron. It represented an original name Bunga.
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, The Lord of the Rings, Appendix F, "On Translation"

claims.text: Bungo was the eldest child of Mungo Baggins and Laura Grubb. He married Belladonna Took, daughter of the Old Took, towards . Bungo and Belladonna had only one child together, the famous Bilbo Baggins.
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, The Lord of the Rings, Appendix C, "Baggins of Hobbiton"

claims.text: Father and son were so much alike, in looks and behaviour, that Bilbo seemed like a "second edition" of his "solid and comfortable" father.
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, The Hobbit, "An Unexpected Party"

claims.text: Apart from fathering Bilbo, Bungo's other achievements were that he built and excavated the rather luxurious Bag End in the Hill in Hobbiton and that he laid down several bottles of Old Winyards wine that would be enjoyed by Rorimac Brandybuck after Bilbo's Farewell Party and by the small party on 21 September that Frodo Baggins gave before leaving Bag End.
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, The Hobbit, "An Unexpected Party"; J.R.R. Tolkien, The Lord of the Rings, The Fellowship of the Ring, "Three is Company"

claims.text: Bungo had an aptitude for either remembering or coining proverbs. Bilbo quoted his father's sayings "third time pays for all" before making his first descent into Erebor, "Every worm has his weak spot" while talking to the Dragon Smaug, and "while there's life there's hope" when leading the Dwarves down to Smaug's lair.
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, The Hobbit, "Inside Information"; J.R.R. Tolkien, The Hobbit, "Not at Home"

claims.text: Nothing is known about the life of Calimmacil, who enters history because after King Ondoher and his sons were slain in battle, his grandson Eärnil was chosen to succeed Ondoher to the throne.
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, The Lord of the Rings, Appendix A, "The Númenorean Kings", "Gondor and the Heirs of Anárion"

claims.text: Camellia was daughter of the head of the Sackville Family. She married Longo Baggins, and had one son, Otho. The double surname Sackville-Baggins was bestowed on her son, after the death of Camellia's father, as he was the eldest grandson, and became the new head.
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, The Lord of the Rings, Appendix C, "Baggins of Hobbiton"; J.R.R. Tolkien; Humphrey Carpenter, Christopher Tolkien (eds.), The Letters of J.R.R. Tolkien, Letter 214, (undated, written late 1958 or early 1959)

claims.text:
In early sketches of the Family Trees, Camellia was said to be from Michel Delving.

claims.text: Carandrian was a friend of Quickbeam, and one of the Ents that took part in the Battle of Isengard; during the battle he was injured by an axe, which enraged the rest of the Ents.
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), The War of the Ring, "Part One: The Fall of Saruman", "IV. Flotsam and Jetsam", pp. 54-5

claims.text:
Physically, Caranthir was notable for two characteristics: his exceptionally dark hair (inherited from his father's side) and his ruddy complexion (inherited from his mother's side). These became the bases of his father-name and mother-name respectively.
Caranthir's personality was noted as being harsh, haughty, and quick to anger. His words to Angrod not only diminished the standing of the House of Fëanor at the early council of the Noldor, but remained with Angrod, and the bitterness of them contributed to his confessing the deeds of the Noldor to Thingol many years later.
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), The War of the Jewels, "Part One. The Grey Annals": §104

claims.text: Caranthir is the Sindarized form of Carnistir, being a compound of caran (“red”) and þir ("face").
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, "From The Shibboleth of Fëanor" (edited by Carl F. Hostetter), in Vinyar Tengwar, Number 41, July 2000, p. 10

claims.text: In , the first Men in Beleriand were encountered in Ossiriand by Finrod. As the Green-elves of that region were troubled by them, Finrod persuaded them to carry onward, and they settled in Estolad. Soon after, in , a second group of Men, the Haladin, arrived and, after they met the unfriendship of the Green-elves, they turned north and settled in Thargelion where the people of Caranthir paid little heed to them.
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), The War of the Jewels, "Part Two. The Later Quenta Silmarillion: Of the Coming of Men into the West (Chapter 14)", p. §13

claims.text: At this Angrod became exceedingly wroth and left the council. And though Maedhros rebuked Caranthir, his words troubled the hearts of the Noldor, who feared that the sons of Fëanor would ever be like to burst forth in rash word or violence. Thus, when it came to selecting an overlord of the Exiles, all save few chose Fingolfin. Maedhros then subsequently waived his claim to the title, and shortly after relocated the House of Fëanor to East Beleriand.
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), The War of the Jewels, "Part One. The Grey Annals": §§65-69

claims.text: The people of Caranthir took the easternmost area which lay between the river Gelion and the Blue Mountains and fortified the mountains east of Maglor's Gap. In the valley between Mount Rerir and the Blue Mountains, shadowed by them in all directions save the south, lay Lake Helevorn, and it was here that Caranthir had his abode. On the western slope of Mount Rerir itself was constructed a fortress.
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), The Lost Road and Other Writings, "Part Two: Valinor and Middle-earth before The Lord of the Rings, VI. Quenta Silmarillion", p. §118; J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), The Lost Road and Other Writings, "Part Two: Valinor and Middle-earth before The Lord of the Rings, VI. Quenta Silmarillion", p. §142

claims.text: The Sindar had previously called this area Talath Rhúnen ("East Vale"), however the Noldor referred to it as Thargelion ("(Land) beyond Gelion") or Dor Caranthir ("Land of Caranthir").
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), The Lost Road and Other Writings, "Part Two: Valinor and Middle-earth before The Lord of the Rings, VI. Quenta Silmarillion", p. §118

claims.text: In about the people of Caranthir first climbed the Blue Mountains and gazed eastward unto Eriador, which to them seemed wide and wild. They soon after made contact with the Dwarves of the Blue Mountains, who had ceased their traffic into Beleriand since the onslaught of Morgoth and the coming of the Noldor.
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), The War of the Jewels, "Part One. The Grey Annals": §114
claims.section: section == History == > Interaction with the Dwarves

claims.text: There was little love between them, for the Dwarves were secretive and quick to resentment, and Caranthir was haughty and scarce concealed his scorn for their unlovely appearance, and his people followed their lord. Yet, as they both feared and hated Morgoth, alliance was made and from it both had great profit. The smiths and masons of the Dwarves learned many secrets of craft from the Noldor, making them renowned among their kin, while the Noldor obtained great wealth of iron and their armouries became filled with weapons and harness of war. Further, until the power of Maedhros was overthrown, all Dwarven traffic first passed through the hands of Caranthir, and from this he won great riches.
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), The War of the Jewels, "Part One. The Grey Annals": §114
claims.section: section == History == > Interaction with the Dwarves

claims.text: Due to Caranthir's friendship with the Dwarves of Belegost, Eöl in turn much more often visited Nogrod.
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), The War of the Jewels, "Part Three. The Wanderings of Húrin and Other Writings not forming part of the Quenta Silmarillion: III. Maeglin"
claims.section: section == History == > Interaction with the Dwarves

claims.text: After the battle, the power of the sons of Fëanor was broken. Their realms and fortresses in East Beleriand were taken and garrisoned by Orcs, and they retreated to into the woods.
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), The War of the Jewels, "Part One. The Grey Annals": §242
claims.section: section == History == > Last deeds in Beleriand

claims.text: In , he perished along with his brothers Celegorm and Curufin during the Second Kinslaying, the attack by the sons of Fëanor on Menegroth in an attempt to recover a Silmaril from King Dior Eluchíl of Doriath.
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), The Silmarillion, "Quenta Silmarillion: Of the Ruin of Doriath"
claims.section: section == History == > Last deeds in Beleriand

claims.text: Caranthir was a Noldorin prince, one of the seven sons of Fëanor and Nerdanel, born in Valinor during the Time of the Two Trees. His appearance was notable, being as black-haired as of his grandfather Finwë, but having the ruddy complexion of his mother. At some point he married, but nothing of his wife or their family is known.
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), The Peoples of Middle-earth, "XI. The Shibboleth of Fëanor", "The names of the Sons of Fëanor"; J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), The Peoples of Middle-earth, "X. Of Dwarves and Men", "Notes"

claims.text: Fëanor and his sons abode seldom in one place for long, but travelled far and wide upon the confines of Valinor, going even to the borders of the Dark and the cold shores of the Outer Sea, seeking the unknown. Often they were guests in the halls of Aulë.
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), The Silmarillion, "Quenta Silmarillion: Of Eldamar and the Princes of the Eldalië"

claims.text: During the unrest of the Noldor and the strife between Fëanor and his half-brother Fingolfin, Fëanor was banished from Tirion and took up residence in Formenos; he was followed by his father, King Finwë, and his sons.
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), The Silmarillion, "Quenta Silmarillion: Of the Silmarils and the Unrest of the Noldor"

claims.text: They then sped to the Ring of Doom where Maedhros informed Manwë and, unknowingly, also Fëanor who kept himself hidden during the conversation. Fëanor reacted by cursing both Melkor and the summons of Manwë, and then fleeing into the night; the sons of Fëanor followed him, dismayed that he might slay himself.
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), Morgoth's Ring, "Part Three. The Later Quenta Silmarillion: (II) The Second Phase: Of the Rape of the Silmarils", §§7-12

claims.text: After a long march northwards, the Noldor drew close to the Helcaraxë, a land bridge deemed impassable, and the narrow strait between Aman and Middle-earth they intended to sail. With too few ships remaining to ferry all the Noldor at once, and the fear of treachery between their houses, Fëanor and his sons stole away in them, abandoning the host of Fingolfin.
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), The Silmarillion, "Quenta Silmarillion: Of the Flight of the Noldor"

claims.text: After landing at the Firth of Drengist, and burning the ships to prevent any from sailing back, Fëanor's host traveled north and encamped on the northern shore of Lake Mithrim where they were attacked unaware by a host of Morgoth. In the battle that followed, Fëanor's forces were swiftly victorious, and pursued the routed orcs over the Mountains of Shadow into Ard-galen.
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), The Silmarillion, "Quenta Silmarillion: Of the Return of the Noldor"

claims.text: Though Morgoth's assaulting forces were destroyed, Fëanor recklessly drew far ahead of his host in pursuit of the remnant orcs, and was ambushed and mortally wounded at the confines of Dor Daedeloth. He was rescued by his sons, and just before his death he laid it on them to uphold their oath and to avenge him. Shortly after, Maedhros was taken captive after feigning to treat with Morgoth.
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), The Silmarillion, "Quenta Silmarillion: Of the Return of the Noldor"

claims.text: The host of Fëanor remained at northern shore of Lake Mithrim until the arrival of Fingolfin's host, having successfully crossed the Helcaraxë, with the first sunrise in . To avoid open hostilities with Fingolfin's larger forces, the remaining sons of Fëanor relocated to the southern shore of Lake Mithrim. The hatred between the houses began to be assuaged in , when Maedhros was rescued by Fingolfin's son Fingon.
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), The War of the Jewels, "Part One. The Grey Annals": §59; J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), The War of the Jewels, "Part One. The Grey Annals": §61

claims.text: In , Morgoth broke the Siege of Angband with a massive assault against the Noldor. The Orcs broke through the Pass of Aglon and, led by the dragon Glaurung, breached Maglor's Gap. They took the fortress upon the west slopes of Mount Rerir, ravaged all Thargelion, defiled Lake Helevorn and came far into East Beleriand. Caranthir fled and joined the remnant of his people to the scattered folk of Amrod and Amras. They then retreated to the south and established a watch and some strength of war upon Amon Ereb where they had aid of the Green-elves.
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), The War of the Jewels, "Part One. The Grey Annals": §148; J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), The Lost Road and Other Writings, "Part Two: Valinor and Middle-earth before The Lord of the Rings, VI. Quenta Silmarillion", p. §142

claims.text: But the Orcs came not into Ossiriand or South Beleriand. At some point prior to , Morgoth's army in East Beleriand was broken by Thingol on the borders of Doriath. Part had fled away south never to return to him, part retreated north and was stricken by Maedhros, and those that ventured near the mountains were hunted by the Dwarves.
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), The Lost Road and Other Writings, "Part Two: Valinor and Middle-earth before The Lord of the Rings, VI. Quenta Silmarillion", p. §142; J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), The War of the Jewels, "Part One. The Grey Annals": §170

claims.text: In Swarthy Men came out of Eriador, passing north of the Blue Mountains, and entered into Lothlann. They were not unexpected, as Maedhros had been warned by the Dwarves of their coming from out of the further East. They were not a unified people, having many houses with little love among them. But Maedhros, seeing the weakness of the Elves and Edain, and the seemingly inexhaustible store of Angband, made alliance with them and gave them dwellings. Among these Men, the two chieftains with the greatest followings were Bór and Ulfang. While Bór swore loyalty to Maedhros and Maglor, and was presumably given lands within Lothlann, the folk of Ulfang were given lands within Thargelion, and he and his sons, Uldor, Ulfast, and Ulwarth, swore allegiance to Caranthir.
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), The War of the Jewels, "Part One. The Grey Annals": §§173-174

claims.text: In , following the successful Quest of the Silmaril, new hope arose that Morgoth was not unconquerable, and the Union of Maedhros was formed. Among these preparations, the Men of Bór and of Ulfang were marshalled and trained for war, and given fair arms, and they summoned yet more of their kinsfolk out of the East. In spring of the following year, the Union made its first trial of strength, and soon succeeded in driving the Orcs out of Beleriand and reestablishing the frontiers as they had been during the Siege.
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), The War of the Jewels, "Part One. The Grey Annals": §212; J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), The War of the Jewels, "Part One. The Grey Annals": §213

claims.text:
Caranthir had the sobriquet of "the dark".
Caranthir's father-name was Morifinwë ("Dark Finwë"), for he was black-haired as his grandfather. The short form of this name was Moryo.
His mother-name was Carnistir ("Red-face") which was a compound of carnë and stîre.
In Ælfwine’s translation of the Quenta into Old English; Old English equivalents of Elvish names, his name is given as Colþegn Nihthelm and defined as "[Cranthir the Dark. O.E. col 'coal', þegn 'thane'; niht-helm lit. 'night-helm', but poetically referring to 'cover of night']"
An earlier variant of his name was Cranthir (N. "perfect"); it was alternatively spelled as Cranthor.
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), The Silmarillion, "Quenta Silmarillion: Of Eldamar and the Princes of the Eldalië"; J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), The Peoples of Middle-earth, "XI. The Shibboleth of Fëanor", "The names of the Sons of Fëanor"; J.R.R. Tolkien, "From The Shibboleth of Fëanor" (edited by Carl F. Hostetter), in Vinyar Tengwar, Number 41, July 2000, p. 10; J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), The Shaping of Middle-earth, "III. The Quenta: Appendix 1: Fragments of a translation of The Quenta Noldorinwa into Old English, made by Ælfwine or Eriol; together with Old English equivalents of Elvish names"; J.R.R. Tolkien, "The Alphabet of Rúmil & Early Noldorin Fragments", in Parma Eldalamberon XIII (edited by Carl F. Hostetter, Christopher Gilson, Arden R. Smith, Patrick H. Wynne, and Bill Welden), p. 161

claims.text:
In The Nauglafring, from the second volume of The History of Middle-earth, the only mention of Cranthor is the attack on Dior's realm to reclaim the Silmaril, and his subsequent death beside Celegorm.
In The Lay of the Children of Húrin, from the third volume, Flinding (Gwindor) tells Túrin about the Sons of Fëanor who live secretly in the forests of the East as unflinching foes of Morgoth, including "dark Cranthir".
In The Earliest 'Silmarillion', from the fourth volume, an early version has the Sons of Fëanor succeed in recovering the Silmaril after attacking Doriath and slaying Dior; however, owing to the curse of the gold, they then quarrelled for it, until only Maglor was left. This was very soon after emended to Elwing escaping with the Silmaril.
In The Earliest Annals of Beleriand, from the fourth volume, the sons of Ulfand (Uldor, Ulfast, and Ulwar) were most beloved by Cranthir among Sons of Fëanor, and they swore fealty to him. In the Battle of Unnumbered Tears, Uldor betrayed the Sons of Fëanor to Morgoth, and fell on their right flank. It was Cranthir who then slew Uldor.
In one version of the Battle of Sarn Athrad, the Dwarf army (likely of Nogrod) was defeated and "almost entirely destroyed by Caranthir".
While in the published Silmarillion Caranthir is recorded as the fourth son of Fëanor, in The Shibboleth of Fëanor Curufin is explicitly numbered as the fourth. This would then imply Caranthir to be the fifth son instead.
In The Nature of Middle-earth, a footnote regarding Finrod's epessë, Felegund, states that "This nick-name was probably actually given to Finrod not by Dwarves but by the Sons of Fëanor at least partly in derision. There was no great love between the Sons of Fëanor and the children of Finarphin, though they hid their enmity at need. (As when Curufin and Caranthir dwelt in the shelter of Nargothrond after the defeat of the Elves by Morgoth in the North). Moreover the Sons of Fëanor had much communication with the Dwarves of Nogrod and Belegost." It may be assumed that this was intended to refer to Celegorm instead.

claims.text: In The Nauglafring, from the second volume of The History of Middle-earth, the only mention of Cranthor is the attack on Dior's realm to reclaim the Silmaril, and his subsequent death beside Celegorm.
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), The Book of Lost Tales Part Two, "IV. The Nauglafring"
claims.section: section == Other versions of the legendarium ==

claims.text: In The Lay of the Children of Húrin, from the third volume, Flinding (Gwindor) tells Túrin about the Sons of Fëanor who live secretly in the forests of the East as unflinching foes of Morgoth, including "dark Cranthir".
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), The Lays of Beleriand, "I. The Lay of the Children of Húrin: III. Failivrin"
claims.section: section == Other versions of the legendarium ==

claims.text: In The Earliest 'Silmarillion', from the fourth volume, an early version has the Sons of Fëanor succeed in recovering the Silmaril after attacking Doriath and slaying Dior; however, owing to the curse of the gold, they then quarrelled for it, until only Maglor was left. This was very soon after emended to Elwing escaping with the Silmaril.
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), The Shaping of Middle-earth, "II. The Earliest 'Silmarillion' (The 'Sketch of the Mythology')"
claims.section: section == Other versions of the legendarium ==

claims.text: In The Earliest Annals of Beleriand, from the fourth volume, the sons of Ulfand (Uldor, Ulfast, and Ulwar) were most beloved by Cranthir among Sons of Fëanor, and they swore fealty to him. In the Battle of Unnumbered Tears, Uldor betrayed the Sons of Fëanor to Morgoth, and fell on their right flank. It was Cranthir who then slew Uldor.
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), The Shaping of Middle-earth, "VII. The Earliest Annals of Beleriand"
claims.section: section == Other versions of the legendarium ==

claims.text: In one version of the Battle of Sarn Athrad, the Dwarf army (likely of Nogrod) was defeated and "almost entirely destroyed by Caranthir".
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), The War of the Jewels, "Part Three. The Wanderings of Húrin and Other Writings not forming part of the Quenta Silmarillion: V. The Tale of Years"
claims.section: section == Other versions of the legendarium ==

claims.text: While in the published Silmarillion Caranthir is recorded as the fourth son of Fëanor, in The Shibboleth of Fëanor Curufin is explicitly numbered as the fourth. This would then imply Caranthir to be the fifth son instead.
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), The Peoples of Middle-earth, "XI. The Shibboleth of Fëanor", "The names of the Sons of Fëanor"

claims.text: Born in , Carl and his siblings spent much time in Bywater, and would often swim in the Bywater Pool with the Gamgee children. He had not yet come of age when Sharkey's Ruffians entered the Shire, so his father ordered him to guard the house with a pitch fork while his father and brothers fought in the Battle of Bywater.
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, The Lord of the Rings, Appendix C, "The Longfather-tree of Master Samwise"; J.R.R. Tolkien, The Lord of the Rings, The Return of the King, "Mount Doom"; J.R.R. Tolkien, The Lord of the Rings, The Return of the King, "The Scouring of the Shire"

claims.text: When Eldacar ascended to the throne in a civil war broke out in Gondor. Eldacar's mother had been Vidumavi, a princess from Rhovanion and not of Númenórean descent. It was unheard of for an heir to the throne to come from one of an alien and lesser race, as viewed by the Dúnedain, and many feared that her shorter lifespan would diminish the majesty of the Kings. Before Eldacar's ascension rebellion brewed in Gondor, especially in the southern parts, and when he became King full civil war broke out, called the Kin-strife.
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, The Lord of the Rings, Appendix B, "The Third Age"

claims.text: However, Castamir's sons escaped from the battle and withdrew their father's forces into Pelargir. There they withstood a siege until they could sail away to Umbar. This city and haven became a lordship independent of Gondor and a refuge for all enemies of the realm, a threat that would last for centuries.
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, The Lord of the Rings, Appendix A, "The Númenorean Kings", "Gondor and the Heirs of Anárion"

claims.text: Celandine was descended from the line of the Masters of the Hall of Buckland: specifically, from Gorbadoc Brandybuck. Along with her parents and her brothers Doderic and Ilberic, she was present at Bilbo's Farewell Party.
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, The Lord of the Rings, Appendix C, "Brandybuck of Buckland"

claims.text:
Celeborn is a Sindarin name, consisting of celeb ("silver") + a derivative of ornā ("tall"). Teleporno, his original Telerin name, has an identical meaning. The name Teleporno was "Sindarized" as Celeborn: Telerin telpe ("silver") (Quenya tyelpe) was transformed to Sindarin celeb. Teleporno's name gained an additional Quenya form, Telporno (pron. ).
He was given the epithet "the Wise" by Galadriel.
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), Unfinished Tales, "The History of Galadriel and Celeborn", "Appendix E: The Names of Celeborn and Galadriel"; J.R.R. Tolkien; Humphrey Carpenter, Christopher Tolkien (eds.), The Letters of J.R.R. Tolkien, Letter 347, (dated 17 December 1972); J.R.R. Tolkien, The Lord of the Rings, The Fellowship of the Ring, "The Mirror of Galadriel", twenty-fifth paragraph

claims.text: Celeborn is a Sindarin name, consisting of celeb ("silver") + a derivative of ornā ("tall"). Teleporno, his original Telerin name, has an identical meaning. The name Teleporno was "Sindarized" as Celeborn: Telerin telpe ("silver") (Quenya tyelpe) was transformed to Sindarin celeb. Teleporno's name gained an additional Quenya form, Telporno (pron. ).
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), Unfinished Tales, "The History of Galadriel and Celeborn", "Appendix E: The Names of Celeborn and Galadriel"; J.R.R. Tolkien; Humphrey Carpenter, Christopher Tolkien (eds.), The Letters of J.R.R. Tolkien, Letter 347, (dated 17 December 1972)

claims.text: He was given the epithet "the Wise" by Galadriel.
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, The Lord of the Rings, The Fellowship of the Ring, "The Mirror of Galadriel", twenty-fifth paragraph

claims.text: Silver, long
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, The Lord of the Rings, The Fellowship of the Ring, "The Mirror of Galadriel"

claims.text: In the late First Age, Finrod and Galadriel came to Doriath as guests of Thingol. There, Celeborn and Galadriel met, fell in love, and were soon betrothed. Galadriel remained in Doriath with Celeborn after Finrod went to the Caverns of Narog to establish the stronghold of Nargothrond.
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), The Silmarillion, "Quenta Silmarillion: Of the Return of the Noldor"

claims.text: For the rest of the First Age, Celeborn and Galadriel are not mentioned to have played any significant role in the general course of events of the Age, while their relatives, both Sindar and Noldor, did. By the Fall of Nargothrond in , Galadriel passed over the Blue Mountains so it seems likely that Celeborn followed her although this is not known for certain.
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, The Lord of the Rings, The Fellowship of the Ring, "The Mirror of Galadriel"

claims.text: After Galadriel's departure, it is believed that Celeborn relocated to Rivendell to reside with Elladan, Elrohir, and some of the Noldor, having also grown weary of East Lórien.
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, The Lord of the Rings, "Prologue", "Note on the Shire Records"; J.R.R. Tolkien, The Lord of the Rings, Appendix B, "The Great Years"

claims.text: At some unknown date (possibly between and ), he sought the Grey Havens and sailed west aboard Last Ship with his mighty kinsman Cirdan the Shipwright, but when he did so, he took with him the last memory of the Elder Days in Middle-earth.
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, The Lord of the Rings, "Prologue", "Note on the Shire Records"

claims.text: After the fall of Beleriand, Celeborn and Galadriel lived in Lindon for some time. Celeborn ruled the fief of Harlindon, which was composed mostly of Sindar, under High King Gil-galad.
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), The Peoples of Middle-earth, "Of Dwarves and Men"

claims.text: Galadriel and Celeborn crossed into Eriador with many Noldor, Sindar, and Green-elves in their following. For a while, they dwelt in the country about Lake Nenuial, ruling the Eldar in Eriador, including the wandering companies of the native Nandor. Probably around , a daughter was born to Galadriel and Celeborn, named Celebrían. They departed for Eregion and arrived there by . It was ruled by Celebrimbor, grandson of Fëanor and the distant half-cousin of Galadriel.
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, Carl F. Hostetter (ed.), "Part One. Time and Ageing: IX. Time-scales and Rates of Growth", The Nature of Middle-earth, HarperCollins, 2021, calculation for Galadriel in a manuscript from c. 1959, p. 65; J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), Unfinished Tales, "The History of Galadriel and Celeborn", "Concerning Galadriel and Celeborn"; J.R.R. Tolkien, "Notes and Translations", The Road Goes Ever On

claims.text: It was only sometime between and that Galadriel crossed the Hithaeglir through Khazad-dûm and relocated there with their daughter Celebrían, becoming great among the Wood-elves. Celeborn decided to stay in Eregion due to his enmity towards the Dwarves. It is said that Celeborn fought in the Sack of Eregion leading the remnants of Eregion out of the battle. He and Elrond narrowly escaped to a dell, where the latter founded Rivendell.
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), Unfinished Tales, "The History of Galadriel and Celeborn", "Concerning Galadriel and Celeborn"

claims.text: After the War of the Elves and Sauron, Galadriel passed again through Moria with Celebrían and came to Imladris, seeking Celeborn. There she found him, and there they dwelt together for a long time. Some time later, Galadriel and Celeborn departed from Imladris and went to the little-inhabited lands between the mouth of the Gwathló and Ethir Anduin. There they dwelt in Belfalas, at the place that was afterwards called Dol Amroth; and their company was swelled by Silvan Elves from Lórinand.
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), Unfinished Tales, "The History of Galadriel and Celeborn", "Concerning Galadriel and Celeborn"

claims.text: During the War of the Ring in , Lothlórien received the Fellowship of the Ring, composed of various travellers on the quest to destroy the One Ring. Celeborn and Galadriel offered advice and boats for the Anduin, sending them on their way. After the Galadhrim repelled the forces of Dol Guldur three times, Celeborn led the forces of the Galadhrim across the Anduin and took the fortress. Galadriel threw down its walls and purified the forest.
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, The Lord of the Rings, Appendix B, "The Great Years"; J.R.R. Tolkien, The Lord of the Rings, Appendix B, "The Chief Days from the Fall of Barad-dûr to the End of the Third Age"

claims.text: On 6 April, that was the Elven day of New Year, Thranduil met with Celeborn in the midst of Mirkwood and renamed it Eryn Lasgalen, "The Wood of the Green Leaves". With the forest now cleansed, it was divided among the Elves and Men; Celeborn took all the forest south of the Narrows and established East Lórien.
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, The Lord of the Rings, Appendix B, "The Chief Days from the Fall of Barad-dûr to the End of the Third Age"; J.R.R. Tolkien, The Lord of the Rings, Appendix B, "The Great Years"

claims.text: Celeborn attended the wedding of Aragorn II Elessar and his granddaughter Arwen, and on the journey to return, he bade a fond farewell to Treebeard as well. He and Galadriel escorted Gandalf and the Hobbits until the Mountains of Moria, and on 13 September they turned to return to Lothlórien.
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, The Lord of the Rings, Appendix B, "The Chief Days from the Fall of Barad-dûr to the End of the Third Age"

claims.text: Before the summer of 1950 in an earlier version of the Appendix on Languages it was mentioned that the native language of Celeborn was Telerian, the native language of the Teleri who remained behind in the north-west of Middle-earth, of the Elves of Lórien and of the elf-kingdom in Northern Mirkwood of Thranduil, and that in the household of Galadriel also Noldorin was spoken, because she was a Noldo. It thus appears that Celeborn was a wood-elf in this earlier version. In a later version of the Appendix on Languages following a major revision of 1951, it is first mentioned that Celeborn was a Sinda (Grey-elf) and that most of the people of Lórien were of a woodland race. The text in the final version of The Lord of the Rings only mentions that Celeborn was a kinsman of Thingol. The Lord of the Rings does not mention the ancestry of Celeborn and if he was a Sinda or a Teler from Valinor. The text in The Silmarillion also only mentions that Celeborn was a kinsman of Thingol and that Galadriel stayed in Doriath, because Celeborn lived there and did not accompany her brother Finrod to Nargothrond, and that Celeborn was a prince of Doriath and calls him Celeborn of Doriath. The Silmarillion leaves the ancestry of Celeborn open and there is no mention if he was a Sinda or Teler, only implying that Galadriel met Celeborn in Doriath.
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), The Peoples of Middle-earth, "II. The Appendix on Languages", manuscript F 2, §18, p. 36 and §3 - §5, commentary §18, pp. 65-66; J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), The Peoples of Middle-earth, "II. The Appendix on Languages", typescript F4; J.R.R. Tolkien, The Lord of the Rings, Appendix B, "The Second Age", second paragraph; J.R.R. Tolkien, The Lord of the Rings, Appendix F, "The Languages and Peoples of the Third Age", "Of the Elves" third paragraph mentioning that the Exiles had adopted Sindarin and that Galadriel was the noblest of all; J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), The Silmarillion, "Quenta Silmarillion: Of the Return of the Noldor"; J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), The Silmarillion, "Quenta Silmarillion: Of the Ruin of Doriath"; J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), The Silmarillion, "Quenta Silmarillion: Of the Voyage of Eärendil and the War of Wrath"; J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), The Silmarillion, "Of the Rings of Power and the Third Age"
claims.section: section == Other versions of the legendarium == > As a Sinda

claims.text: In a table with the descendants of Thingol from December 1959 Thingol's younger brother Elmo has a son Galadhon who has two sons, Celeborn and Galathil, and a daughter, Nimloth, who married King Dior. However, on the same table Nimloth also appears as the daughter of Galathil. It looks as if the second thought of J.R.R. Tolkien was that Nimloth was the daughter of Galathil and the niece of Celeborn. The genealogy according to this second thought was included in Unfinished Tales. According to that table, Celeborn is thus the greatnephew of Thingol and second cousin of Galadriel.
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), The War of the Jewels, "Part Three. The Wanderings of Húrin and Other Writings not forming part of the Quenta Silmarillion: V. The Tale of Years", stage 'D', p. 257; J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), Unfinished Tales, "The History of Galadriel and Celeborn", last paragraph before the section Concerning Galadriel and Celeborn, p. 233
claims.section: section == Other versions of the legendarium == > As a Sinda

claims.text: In a text written in 1965, Celeborn is born in Beleriand and he is a descendant of Elmo. In a rejected note he is the father of Amroth, and was left with his son after his (first) wife stole away and deserted them. Tolkien further noted that while remarriage seldom happened, it could occur in the time of such divided feelings as of the end of the First Age.
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, Carl F. Hostetter (ed.), "Part One. Time and Ageing: XVIII. Elvish Ages & Númenórean", The Nature of Middle-earth, HarperCollins, 2021; J.R.R. Tolkien, Carl F. Hostetter (ed.), "Part One. Time and Ageing: XVIII. Elvish Ages & Númenórean", The Nature of Middle-earth, HarperCollins, 2021, p. note 6
claims.section: section == Other versions of the legendarium == > As a Sinda

claims.text: Only a note in The Road Goes Ever On, which was published in 1967 during J.R.R. Tolkien's lifetime, strictly mentions that Celeborn was a Sinda.
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, "Notes and Translations", The Road Goes Ever On, p. 60
claims.section: section == Other versions of the legendarium == > As a Sinda

claims.text: According to an alternate history of Celeborn and Galadriel in Unfinished Tales, Celeborn was a Teler of noble rank in Alqualondë, born Teleporno, grandson of Olwë, prince of Alqualondë (thus he was a kinsman of Thingol in Beleriand). Only nine months before his death, J.R.R. Tolkien still was of the opinion that Celeborn was only a kinsman of Thingol afar off, because Celeborn came from Valinor and that his orginal name was Telporno.
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), Morgoth's Ring, "Part Two. The Annals of Aman: Commentary on the fifth section of the Annals of Aman", notes and corrections, §149; J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), The Peoples of Middle-earth, "XI. The Shibboleth of Fëanor", pp. 347, 364 (note 46); J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), Unfinished Tales, "The History of Galadriel and Celeborn", eighteenth paragraph; J.R.R. Tolkien; Humphrey Carpenter, Christopher Tolkien (eds.), The Letters of J.R.R. Tolkien, Letter 347, (dated 17 December 1972), answer to question 3
claims.section: section == Other versions of the legendarium == > As a Teler

claims.text: In one c. 1969 version of the legendarium, Celeborn was the son of a Telerin Elf called Gilitīro.
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, "Eldarin Pronouns", in Parma Eldalamberon XXIII (edited by Christopher Gilson), p. 143
claims.section: section == Other versions of the legendarium == > As a Teler

claims.text: Artanis, Olwë's granddaughter and a Noldorin princess of great beauty, often spent long visits to Alqualondë and her mother’s kin. During this time the two fell in love, and Teleporno gave her the romantic epithet Alatáriel, meaning "Maiden Crowned with Radiant Garland".
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), The Peoples of Middle-earth, "XI. The Shibboleth of Fëanor"
claims.section: section == Other versions of the legendarium == > As a Teler

claims.text: Later, Teleporno and Artanis helped to defend Alqualondë from the Noldor during the First Kinslaying. Nevertheless, Artanis’s heart was fired by the stories of Fëanor of the open lands across the sea. She urged Teleporno to take a ship eastward to Endor, and he gave in. In doing so the two fell under the Ban of the Valar.
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), Morgoth's Ring, "Part Two. The Annals of Aman: Commentary on the fifth section of the Annals of Aman", notes and corrections, §149; J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), Unfinished Tales, "The History of Galadriel and Celeborn", eighteenth paragraph
claims.section: section == Other versions of the legendarium == > As a Teler

claims.text: Celeborn's Telerin ancestry would have made the couple first cousins. Morgoth's Ring states that among the Eldar first cousins might marry, but seldom did so or desired to do so. Furthermore, the published Silmarillion states "Eldar wedded not with kin so near," in reference to Maeglin's attraction to his first cousin Idril.
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), Morgoth's Ring, "Part Three. The Later Quenta Silmarillion: (II) The Second Phase: Laws and Customs among the Eldar"; J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), The Silmarillion, "Quenta Silmarillion: Of Maeglin"
claims.section: section == Other versions of the legendarium == > As a Teler

claims.text: Celebrían is a Sindarin name, which means "Silver queen". It is probably a compound of celeb ("silver") and rían ("queen").
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien; Humphrey Carpenter, Christopher Tolkien (eds.), The Letters of J.R.R. Tolkien, Letter 345, (dated 30 November 1972), p. 423

claims.text: Celebrían was born early in the Second Age, likely in , when Galadriel refused to return to Eressëa, and passed over the Mountains. Celebrían lived in Eregion, and later moved to Lórien with her mother in . In , she went to Rivendell with Galadriel searching for Celeborn, where she first met Lord Elrond, who loved her in secret. Their marriage was delayed by the wars against Sauron, though they would eventually wed in . Their first children, the twins Elladan and Elrohir, were born in , and their daughter Arwen in . She had inherited the Elfstone from her mother, which was later given to Arwen, her daughter.
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, Carl F. Hostetter (ed.), "Part One. Time and Ageing: IX. Time-scales and Rates of Growth", The Nature of Middle-earth, HarperCollins, 2021, p. 65; J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), Unfinished Tales, "The History of Galadriel and Celeborn", "Concerning Galadriel and Celeborn", pp. 234, 240; J.R.R. Tolkien, Carl F. Hostetter (ed.), "Part One. Time and Ageing: XVIII. Elvish Ages & Númenórean", The Nature of Middle-earth, HarperCollins, 2021, p. 135; J.R.R. Tolkien, The Lord of the Rings, Appendix B, "The Third Age", entry for the year 109, p. 1085; J.R.R. Tolkien, The Lord of the Rings, Appendix B, "The Third Age", entries for the years 130 and 241, p. 1085; J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), Unfinished Tales, "The History of Galadriel and Celeborn", "The Elessar", p. 251

claims.text: She was followed by Elrond and her mother Galadriel, who eventually took the White Ship in the end of the Third Age and also passed the Great Sea to the Undying Lands, where they presumably reunited with her. Later Celeborn and possibly her sons, Elladan and Elrohir, also went to the Grey Havens to sail to the Undying Lands, and presumably reunited with Celebrían.
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, The Lord of the Rings, The Return of the King, "The Grey Havens", p. 1029; J.R.R. Tolkien, The Lord of the Rings, "Prologue", "Note on the Shire Records", p. 15

claims.text:
J.R.R. Tolkien tried to define the birth-year of Celebrían in different manuscripts, specially those dealing with chronology and Elven growth. Here are the dates of the Second Age, presented in chronological order as Tolkien considered them: (circa), 300 ("probably"), 260 or , (a proposal while calculating her age), 9 (circa) or 45.
In "Concerning Galadriel and Celeborn" (the only narrative dealing with a complete history of Middle-earth during the Second Age), both Celebrían and Amroth are children of Galadriel and Celeborn, but in later texts J.R.R. Tolkien gave Amroth a Sindarin origin.
In the drafts of The Tale of Years of the Third Age, Elrond married Celebrían c. T.A. 2500 and their children were born in the same century. In , she was slain by Orcs instead of captured. The marriage was later changed to 2300, and her capture and departure to 2509.
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, Carl F. Hostetter (ed.), "Part Three. The World, its Lands, and its Inhabitants: XVI. Galadriel and Celeborn", The Nature of Middle-earth, HarperCollins, 2021, p. 346; J.R.R. Tolkien, Carl F. Hostetter (ed.), "Part One. Time and Ageing: IX. Time-scales and Rates of Growth", The Nature of Middle-earth, HarperCollins, 2021, p. 65; J.R.R. Tolkien, Carl F. Hostetter (ed.), "Part One. Time and Ageing: X. Difficulties in Chronology", The Nature of Middle-earth, HarperCollins, 2021, p. 73; J.R.R. Tolkien, Carl F. Hostetter (ed.), "Part One. Time and Ageing: XI. Ageing of Elves", The Nature of Middle-earth, HarperCollins, 2021, pp. 77, 79; J.R.R. Tolkien, Carl F. Hostetter (ed.), "Part One. Time and Ageing: XVIII. The Tale of Years of the Third Age", p. 234–6

claims.text: J.R.R. Tolkien tried to define the birth-year of Celebrían in different manuscripts, specially those dealing with chronology and Elven growth. Here are the dates of the Second Age, presented in chronological order as Tolkien considered them: (circa), 300 ("probably"), 260 or , (a proposal while calculating her age), 9 (circa) or 45.
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, Carl F. Hostetter (ed.), "Part Three. The World, its Lands, and its Inhabitants: XVI. claims.text: In "Concerning Galadriel and Celeborn" (the only narrative dealing with a complete history of Middle-earth during the Second Age), both Celebrían and Amroth are children of Galadriel and Celeborn, but in later texts J.R.R. Tolkien gave Amroth a Sindarin origin.
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), Unfinished Tales, "The History of Galadriel and Celeborn", "Concerning Galadriel and Celeborn", pp. 234, 240; J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), Unfinished Tales, "The History of Galadriel and Celeborn", "Amroth and Nimrodel", p. 244
claims.section: section == Other versions of the legendarium ==

claims.text: In the drafts of The Tale of Years of the Third Age, Elrond married Celebrían c. T.A. 2500 and their children were born in the same century. In , she was slain by Orcs instead of captured. The marriage was later changed to 2300, and her capture and departure to 2509.
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), The Peoples of Middle-earth, "VIII. The Tale of Years of the Third Age", p. 226; J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), The Peoples of Middle-earth, "VIII. The Tale of Years of the Third Age", p. 234–6
claims.section: section == Other versions of the legendarium ==

claims.text:
The name Celebrimbor is in Sindarin, meaning "Silver-fist"; it is comprised of the elements celebrin ("like silver in hue or worth") + paur ("fist, closed hand"), with the ending -bor in Celebrimbor being a suffixal form of paur.
Its Quenya cognate is Telperinquar or Telpinquar.
For another, later etymology that contradicts the origins of the character of Celebrimbor as seen in The Lord of the Rings, see below.
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, "Words, Phrases and Passages in Various Tongues in The Lord of the Rings: Eldarin Roots and Stems", in Parma Eldalamberon XVII (edited by Christopher Gilson), entry S Celebrimbor, p. 42

claims.text:
According to this version of his history, the name Celebrimbor is likewise in Sindarin. However, in this text, Celebrimbor is a Sindarized version of his original Telerin name Telperimpar (with Tyelpinquar being its Quenya cognate).
The name was derived from the root KWAR ("press together, squeeze, wring"), whose derivatives were: quár (Q), pār (T) and paur (S).
The text also says that it was a common name among the Teleri of Aman, who were renowned silver-smiths.
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), The Peoples of Middle-earth, "X. Of Dwarves and Men", "Notes", note 7, pp. 318-9; J.R.R. Tolkien, "Eldarin Hands, Fingers & Numerals and Related Writings — Part One" (edited by Patrick H. Wynne), in Vinyar Tengwar, Number 47, February 2005, entry 4. Q. quár, p. 8; J.R.R. Tolkien, Carl F. Hostetter (ed.), "Part Two. Body, Mind and Spirit: III. Eldarin Hands, Fingers, and Numerals", The Nature of Middle-earth, HarperCollins, 2021, p. 178

claims.text: The name Celebrimbor is in Sindarin, meaning "Silver-fist"; it is comprised of the elements celebrin ("like silver in hue or worth") + paur ("fist, closed hand"), with the ending -bor in Celebrimbor being a suffixal form of paur.
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, "Words, Phrases and Passages in Various Tongues in The Lord of the Rings: Eldarin Roots and Stems", in Parma Eldalamberon XVII (edited by Christopher Gilson), entry S Celebrimbor, p. 42

claims.text: Its Quenya cognate is Telperinquar or Telpinquar.
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, "Words, Phrases and Passages in Various Tongues in The Lord of the Rings: Eldarin Roots and Stems", in Parma Eldalamberon XVII (edited by Christopher Gilson), entry S Celebrimbor, p. 42

claims.text: The text also says that it was a common name among the Teleri of Aman, who were renowned silver-smiths.
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), The Peoples of Middle-earth, "X. Of Dwarves and Men", "Notes", note 7, pp. 318-9; J.R.R. Tolkien, "Eldarin Hands, Fingers & Numerals and Related Writings — Part One" (edited by Patrick H. Wynne), in Vinyar Tengwar, Number 47, February 2005, entry 4. Q. quár, p. 8; J.R.R. Tolkien, Carl F. Hostetter (ed.), "Part Two. Body, Mind and Spirit: III. Eldarin Hands, Fingers, and Numerals", The Nature of Middle-earth, HarperCollins, 2021, p. 178

claims.text: Following the Darkening of Valinor, Celebrimbor followed Fëanor into exile in Middle-earth. His unnamed mother remained behind with the people of Finarfin. Celebrimbor did not swear the Oath of Fëanor. It is unknown whether he took part in the Kinslaying at Alqualondë. It is also unknown whether he crossed the Belegaer in one of the stolen Falmari ships or if he followed Fingolfin across the Helcaraxë.
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), The Silmarillion, "Quenta Silmarillion: Of the Flight of the Noldor", p. 37; J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), The Peoples of Middle-earth, "X. Of Dwarves and Men", "Notes", Note 7, pp. 317-9

claims.text: Celebrimbor's whereabouts in Beleriand in the early Years of the Sun are unattested, but later events suggest that he dwelt with his father Curufin and uncle Celegorm in their realm of Himlad. The realm lasted until the Dagor Bragollach in , in which Morgoth broke the Siege of Angband. After this defeat, Curufin and Celegorm fled to the southwest with many of their people, including Celebrimbor, and took refuge with Finrod Felagund in his realm of Nargothrond.
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), The Silmarillion, "Quenta Silmarillion: Of Beleriand and its Realms", p. 58; J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), The Peoples of Middle-earth, "X. Of Dwarves and Men", "Notes", Note 7, pp. 317-9; J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), The Silmarillion, "Quenta Silmarillion: Of the Ruin of Beleriand and the Fall of Fingolfin"

claims.text: Though they were but refugees and guests in Nargothrond, Curufin and Celegorm sought power, and they quickly gained great influence among the people. For his part, Celebrimbor was not involved in his father's schemes and came to love Finrod.
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), The Peoples of Middle-earth, "X. Of Dwarves and Men", "Notes", Note 7, pp. 317-9

claims.text: In , the brothers' political machinations forced Finrod to surrender his crown to Orodreth and leave his realm. Their dominance would prove short-lived. Later that same year, captives freed from the dungeons of Tol-in-Gaurhoth returned to Nargothrond and spoke against the brothers, revealing their treachery and turning the people against them. Orodreth would not suffer them to be slain and so exiled them from the realm.
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), The War of the Jewels, "Part One. The Grey Annals": §192, p. 65; J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), The Silmarillion, "Quenta Silmarillion: Of Beren and Lúthien"

claims.text: When Celebrimbor learned the truth of his father and uncle's actions, he was "aghast" and parted ways with them. He was not subject to their exile and did not voluntarily follow them. His whereabouts for the remainder of the First Age are unknown.
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), The Peoples of Middle-earth, "X. Of Dwarves and Men", "Notes", Note 7, pp. 317-9

claims.text: The whereabouts of Celebrimbor during the early years of the Second Age are uncertain, but at some point, he became a great friend to Galadriel and Celeborn, and in , Celebrimbor with many others of the exiled Noldor followed them to establish the realm of Eregion near to Khazad-dûm, the mansions of the Longbeard Dwarves. This they did due to the discovery of mithril in the surrounding mountains.
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), The Peoples of Middle-earth, "X. Of Dwarves and Men", "Notes", Note 7, pp. 317-9; J.R.R. Tolkien, The Lord of the Rings, Appendix B, "The Second Age", entry for the year 750, p. 1083; J.R.R. Tolkien, The Lord of the Rings, Appendix B, "The Second Age", p. 1082
claims.section: section == History == > Second Age > Establishment of Eregion and the forging of the Rings of Power

claims.text: Eventually, a great friendship arose between the Elves of Eregion and the Dwarves of Khazad-dûm, such that was never before seen, and Celebrimbor became the Lord of Eregion and the greatest of the Gwaith-i-Mírdain, "People of the Jewel-smiths", who in their skill were second only to Fëanor, Celebrimbor's grandfather. There, Celebrimbor befriended Narvi the Dwarf, who built the Doors of Durin, and Celebrimbor inscribed the words upon it.
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, The Lord of the Rings, Appendix B, "The Second Age", p. 1082; J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), Unfinished Tales, "The History of Galadriel and Celeborn", "Concerning Galadriel and Celeborn"; J.R.R. Tolkien, The Lord of the Rings, The Fellowship of the Ring, "A Journey in the Dark", p. 306
claims.section: section == History == > Second Age > Establishment of Eregion and the forging of the Rings of Power

claims.text: However, in , Sauron, under the fair guise of Annatar, came to Eriador posing as an emissary of the Valar. He was rejected by Gil-galad, the High King of the Noldor, in Lindon (where he was not even admitted to), but although Galadriel did not trust him and treated him with scorn, he was nonetheless accepted by the smiths of Eregion, for Celebrimbor desired in his heart to rival the skill and fame of Fëanor. Galadriel and Celeborn were eventually stripped of their authority in Eregion, and this was largely due to the machinations of Sauron. Galadriel, with her daughter Celebrían, departed for the Elvish realm of Lórien, while Celeborn, due to his dislike of all Dwarves and not wanting to cross through their mansions in Khazad-dûm, remained behind in Eregion, and he was largely ignored by Celebrimbor and Annatar thereafter.
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), Unfinished Tales, "The History of Galadriel and Celeborn", "Concerning Galadriel and Celeborn"
claims.section: section == History == > Second Age > Establishment of Eregion and the forging of the Rings of Power

claims.text: Celebrimbor was ignorant of Sauron's true intentions, and he was unaware that Sauron had incorporated a binding magic into the rings. Furthermore, in secret, Sauron forged the One Ring, a master ring that would rule all the lesser rings, to enable him to rule Middle-earth by controlling those that wore all the other rings. When Sauron placed the One Ring on his finger, claiming dominance over all the Rings of Power and their bearers, the Elves knew his true identity and intentions. Celebrimbor and the Elves of Eregion defied Sauron by withholding the other rings from him. Aside from the One Ring, the greatest rings were created by Celebrimbor himself, and these were never touched by Sauron and thus were uncorrupted by him, although they were still subject to the One Ring. These were the Three Rings of the Elves, and a chief source of the beauty that came about in the Third Age. Celebrimbor named them Vilya, Narya, and Nenya after the Middle-earth elements of air, fire and water. He sent the three rings to Elf-lords for safekeeping: Vilya and Narya to Gil-galad in Lindon; and Nenya to Galadriel. Celebrimbor also sent the mightiest of the seven to Durin III of Khazad-dûm.
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, The Lord of the Rings, Appendix A, "Durin's Folk", p. 1076
claims.section: section == History == > Second Age > The War of the Elves and Sauron and death

claims.text: Sauron retaliated by attacking Eregion, laying waste to the realm. Celebrimbor was captured in the chaos and was forced, under torture, to disclose the locations of the lesser rings, but he would not reveal the whereabouts of the Three. Celebrimbor died from his torment, and his body was shot with arrows and hung upon a pole, and was later paraded as a banner when Sauron attacked the Grey Havens.
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), Unfinished Tales, "The History of Galadriel and Celeborn", "Concerning Galadriel and Celeborn"
claims.section: section == History == > Second Age > The War of the Elves and Sauron and death

claims.text: The first known origin story of Celebrimbor was written by Tolkien in c. 1959, occurring in a text called Concerning Galadriel & Celeborn. There, Celebrimbor was described as an Elf of Gondolin (and one of Turgon's "greatest artificers"), who, after the end of the First Age and the overthrow of Morgoth, became a follower of Celeborn and Galadriel, who were regarded as the "High Lord and Lady of all the Eldar of the West".
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), Unfinished Tales, "The History of Galadriel and Celeborn", "Concerning Galadriel and Celeborn", p. 235; J.R.R. Tolkien, Carl F. Hostetter (ed.), "Part Three. The World, its Lands, and its Inhabitants: XVI. Galadriel and Celeborn", The Nature of Middle-earth, HarperCollins, 2021, p. 347
claims.section: section == Other versions of the legendarium == > Concerning Galadriel & Celeborn and The Elessar

claims.text: In a text titled The Elessar, written at around the same time as that of Concerning Galadriel & Celeborn, Tolkien gives two in-universe accounts of the creation of the Elessar, a gem-stone of which it was said that
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), Unfinished Tales, "The History of Galadriel and Celeborn", "The Elessar", p. 251; J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), Unfinished Tales, "The History of Galadriel and Celeborn", "The Elessar", p. 249
claims.section: section == Other versions of the legendarium == > Concerning Galadriel & Celeborn and The Elessar > The Elessar

claims.text: According to one of these accounts, the original Elessar was made by Enerdhil, a renowned smith of Gondolin, who gave it to Idril the daughter of King Turgon, who in turn gave it to Eärendil her son - and so the original Elessar passed into the West with him on his voyage to Aman.
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), Unfinished Tales, "The History of Galadriel and Celeborn", "The Elessar", p. 249
claims.section: section == Other versions of the legendarium == > Concerning Galadriel & Celeborn and The Elessar > The Elessar

claims.text: Many years later, Galadriel confided in Celebrimbor that she lamented the inevitable decay and diminishment of the lands of Middle-earth, and wished that there was some way to counteract it - because even though she was able to go West to Tol Eressëa, she was still too proud to do so.
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), Unfinished Tales, "The History of Galadriel and Celeborn", "The Elessar", p. 250
claims.section: section == Other versions of the legendarium == > Concerning Galadriel & Celeborn and The Elessar > The Elessar

claims.text: Therefore Celebrimbor, who loved Galadriel (though she "turned to Celeborn of the Trees") began to work on making the second Elessar. Because unbeknownst to Galadriel, Celebrimbor used to be an Elf of Gondolin, and was a friend of Enerdhil, even though Enerdhil "in most things outrivalled him".
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), Unfinished Tales, "The History of Galadriel and Celeborn", "The Elessar", pp. 250-1
claims.section: section == Other versions of the legendarium == > Concerning Galadriel & Celeborn and The Elessar > The Elessar

claims.text: However, even though Celebrimbor managed to make this stone even more "subtle and clear" than that of Enerdhil, due to the ever present influence of Morgoth on Arda even after his defeat in the First Age, the gem's light had less power than the original - because that one captured the light of the Sun in its youth.
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), Unfinished Tales, "The History of Galadriel and Celeborn", "The Elessar", p. 251
claims.section: section == Other versions of the legendarium == > Concerning Galadriel & Celeborn and The Elessar > The Elessar

claims.text: Nonetheless, the Elessar of Celebrimbor was deemed the greatest of his works, save the Three Rings only, and
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), Unfinished Tales, "The History of Galadriel and Celeborn", "The Elessar", p. 251
claims.section: section == Other versions of the legendarium == > Concerning Galadriel & Celeborn and The Elessar > The Elessar

claims.text: According to the final paragraph of The Elessar text, the original Elessar of Celebrimbor (which Idril received) went into the West with Eärendil, and the second one (which Galadriel received) was made by him sometime before Sauron's appearance in Eregion.
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), Unfinished Tales, "The History of Galadriel and Celeborn", "The Elessar", p. 251
claims.section: section == Other versions of the legendarium == > Concerning Galadriel & Celeborn and The Elessar > The Elessar

claims.text: After the establishment of Eregion, Celebrimbor became the "chief craftsman of Eregion" with an "almost 'dwarvish' obsession with crafts", and befriended the Dwarves of Khazad-dûm, of whom a dwarven craftsman called Narvi was his greatest friend - from that friendship both Eregion and Khazad-dûm profited greatly.
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), Unfinished Tales, "The History of Galadriel and Celeborn", "Concerning Galadriel and Celeborn", p. 235
claims.section: section == Other versions of the legendarium == > Concerning Galadriel & Celeborn and The Elessar

claims.text: In c. , Sauron established himself in Mordor, and sent emissaries to Eriador, before finally appearing there himself, in his fairest form, in . However, he was rejected by Gil-galad in Lindon, and after heading to Eregion, was likewise rejected by Galadriel and Celeborn, the original rulers of Eregion in this conception of the legendarium.
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), Unfinished Tales, "The History of Galadriel and Celeborn", "Concerning Galadriel and Celeborn", p. 236
claims.section: section == Other versions of the legendarium == > Concerning Galadriel & Celeborn and The Elessar

claims.text: But even though Celeborn and Galadriel (who he perceived to be his chief obstacle) rejected him, Sauron, posing as an emissary of the Valar, nonetheless managed to convince Celebrimbor and the rest of the Noldorin smiths of Eregion, who by this time have formed a powerful guild called the Gwaith-i-Mírdain, to accept his help in the forging of the Rings of Power; here Tolkien states that the story of Fëanor was repeated.
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), Unfinished Tales, "The History of Galadriel and Celeborn", "Concerning Galadriel and Celeborn", pp. 236-7
claims.section: section == Other versions of the legendarium == > Concerning Galadriel & Celeborn and The Elessar

claims.text: According to a late text called Eldarin Hands, Fingers, and Numerals, from c. 1968, Tolkien changed Celebrimbor's origins from that of a grandson of Fëanor to that of a Teler of Aman (Falmar).
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), The Peoples of Middle-earth, "X. Of Dwarves and Men", "Notes", note 7, pp. 318-9; J.R.R. Tolkien, "Eldarin Hands, Fingers & Numerals and Related Writings — Part One" (edited by Patrick H. Wynne), in Vinyar Tengwar, Number 47, February 2005, entry 4. Q. quár, p. 8; J.R.R. Tolkien, Carl F. Hostetter (ed.), "Part Two. Body, Mind and Spirit: III. Eldarin Hands, Fingers, and Numerals", The Nature of Middle-earth, HarperCollins, 2021, p. 178
claims.section: section == Other versions of the legendarium == > Eldarin Hands, Fingers, and Numerals

claims.text: The text also says that it was a common name among the Teleri of Aman, who were renowned silver-smiths.
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), The Peoples of Middle-earth, "X. Of Dwarves and Men", "Notes", note 7, pp. 318-9; J.R.R. Tolkien, "Eldarin Hands, Fingers & Numerals and Related Writings — Part One" (edited by Patrick H. Wynne), in Vinyar Tengwar, Number 47, February 2005, entry 4. Q. quár, p. 8; J.R.R. Tolkien, Carl F. Hostetter (ed.), "Part Two. Body, Mind and Spirit: III. Eldarin Hands, Fingers, and Numerals", The Nature of Middle-earth, HarperCollins, 2021, p. 178
claims.section: section == Other versions of the legendarium == > Eldarin Hands, Fingers, and Numerals > Etymology

claims.text: During the Second Age, he moved to Eregion due to the rumours of a "marvellous metal" found in Moria, which he named mithril. It is said in the text that
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), The Peoples of Middle-earth, "X. Of Dwarves and Men", "Notes", note 7, pp. 318-9; J.R.R. Tolkien, "Eldarin Hands, Fingers & Numerals and Related Writings — Part One" (edited by Patrick H. Wynne), in Vinyar Tengwar, Number 47, February 2005, entry 4. Q. quár, p. 8; J.R.R. Tolkien, Carl F. Hostetter (ed.), "Part Two. Body, Mind and Spirit: III. Eldarin Hands, Fingers, and Numerals", The Nature of Middle-earth, HarperCollins, 2021, p. 178
claims.section: section == Other versions of the legendarium == > Eldarin Hands, Fingers, and Numerals

claims.text: However, according to his son Christopher, Tolkien most probably forgot the fact that he included Celebrimbor's origins as a descendant of Fëanor in the second edition of The Lord of the Rings (1966), and that, had he remembered it, he would not have changed it.
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), The Peoples of Middle-earth, "X. Of Dwarves and Men", "Notes", note 7, pp. 318-9
claims.section: section == Other versions of the legendarium == > Eldarin Hands, Fingers, and Numerals

claims.text: In a late text that Christopher Tolkien called Of Dwarves and Men (from c. 1969), Tolkien changed Celebrimbor's origins yet again.
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), The Peoples of Middle-earth, "X. Of Dwarves and Men", [Untitled introduction], p. 295; J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), The Peoples of Middle-earth, "X. Of Dwarves and Men", "Notes", note 7, pp. 318-9
claims.section: section == Other versions of the legendarium == > Of Dwarves and Men

claims.text: Here, Celebrimbor is depicted as a Sinda who claimed descent from Daeron, a famous minstrel and the chief loremaster of Doriath. In that text, it is explained how in Eregion, due to the influence of Celebrimbor, the ancient runic alphabet devised by Daeron was, along with Tengwar, also known and used.
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), The Peoples of Middle-earth, "Of Dwarves and Men", p. 297; J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), The Silmarillion, "Quenta Silmarillion: Of the Sindar", p. 43
claims.section: section == Other versions of the legendarium == > Of Dwarves and Men

claims.text: And even though in Eregion these Runes were used mostly on formal occasions, due to the contact between the Elves of Eregion and the Dwarves of Khazad-dûm, and because of the greater ease with which the Runes could be carved on stone, the Longbeard Dwarves adopted and modified them for their own use.
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), The Peoples of Middle-earth, "Of Dwarves and Men", p. 297
claims.section: section == Other versions of the legendarium == > Of Dwarves and Men

claims.text: The character of Celebrimbor first appears in a draft chapter of The Lord of the Rings called The Mines of Moria (from 1939), which would later become the chapter A Journey in the Dark in The Fellowship of the Ring as published.
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), The Return of the Shadow, "The Story Continued: XXV. The Mines of Moria", p. 449; J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), The Treason of Isengard, "XIII. Galadriel", p. 255
claims.section: section == Other versions of the legendarium == > The History of The Lord of the Rings

claims.text: There, as in The Lord of the Rings, he is only mentioned by name when Gandalf was reading the inscription on the Doors of Durin
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), The Return of the Shadow, "The Story Continued: XXV. The Mines of Moria", p. 449
claims.section: section == Other versions of the legendarium == > The History of The Lord of the Rings

claims.text: The name Celebrimbor was also added to The Etymologies, a linguistic work from the late 1930s, at around the same time. There, the name is given under the root KWAR ("clutching hand, fist"), and Celebrimbor's name was explained as meaning "Silver-fist" in Noldorin (which was a precursor language to Sindarin).
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), The Lost Road and Other Writings, Part Three: "The Etymologies", entry KWAR-, p. 366
claims.section: section == Other versions of the legendarium == > The History of The Lord of the Rings

claims.text: Celebrindor was the son of Celepharn, and came to the throne of Arthedain upon his father's death in . His reign as king was uneventful, as relations between the other realms of Arnor - Cardolan and Rhudaur - were good, and no evil threatened the realm yet - it was after Celebrindor's death that Angmar started to pose a threat to the peoples of Arnor.
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, The Lord of the Rings, Appendix A, "The Númenorean Kings", "The Realms in Exile", "The Northern Line: Heirs of Isildur"; J.R.R. Tolkien, The Lord of the Rings, Appendix A, "The Númenorean Kings", "Eriador, Arnor, and the Heirs of Isildur"

claims.text: Celebrindor died in 1272 after ruling the Northern Kingdom for eighty-one years. He was succeeded by his son Malvegil upon his death.
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, The Lord of the Rings, Appendix A, "The Númenorean Kings", "The Realms in Exile", "The Northern Line: Heirs of Isildur"

claims.text:
Celegorm is not glossed, but being the Sindarized version of the Quenya name Tyelkormo, it would mean "Hasty-riser". It is actually North Sindarin, as it keeps the final m.
In the Noldorin phase of the name, it was rendered as Celegorn, presumably meaning "Swift-impetuous".

claims.text:
thumb|left|Grandson of Míriel by ToastedBuckwheat
Celegorm was a Noldorin prince, the third of the seven sons of Fëanor and Nerdanel, born in Valinor during the Time of the Two Trees. Celegorm was a hunter, and a friend of Oromë. He often followed the Oromë’s horn and, while his father and brothers were frequently guests at the halls of Aulë, Celegorm instead went to the house of Oromë where he obtained great knowledge of birds and beasts and learned all their tongues. Oromë further gifted the great wolfhound Huan to Celegorm.
thumb|The Years of Youth by Elena Kukanova
During the unrest of the Noldor, Fëanor forged "fell swords" for his sons, and they followed him to Formenos when he was banished from Tirion. When Morgoth killed Finwë and stole Fëanor's beloved Silmarils, they all took the terrible Oath of Fëanor to recover the jewels, participated in the First Kinslaying at Alqualondë to obtain the Falmari ships, and abandoned the host of Fingolfin when they sailed to Middle-earth.
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), The Silmarillion, "Quenta Silmarillion: Of Eldamar and the Princes of the Eldalië", pg. 97; J.R.R.
