claims.text: Herendil was a daring diver and he was prideful of his talent. In the aftermath of one such dive, his father, Elendil, observes that he seems to have grown drastically and tells Herendil that he has the makings of a fine man.
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), The Lost Road and Other Writings, "Part One: III. The Lost Road, (ii) The Númenórean chapters", pp. 59-61

claims.text: To this, Herendil rebukes his father, believing the comment to be one of mockery, claiming that Elendil knew already that he was of a lesser height than others of his age, and that he was tormented by that. Herendil stated in evidence that he was barely of height to Almáriel's shoulder.
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), The Lost Road and Other Writings, "Part One: III. The Lost Road, (ii) The Númenórean chapters", pp. 59-61

claims.text: Herendil then informed his father that though the two of them are the blood of kings, his peers called him names such as "Terendul" the day prior, and accused him of being a "half-Noldo." Herendil admitted, however, that it is at least better than "being called half a Gnome".
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), The Lost Road and Other Writings, "Part One: III. The Lost Road, (ii) The Númenórean chapters", pp. 59-61

claims.text: Elendil responded saying that then it may be dangerous for Herendil to be his son as his own father's name, Valandil, meant "God-friend".
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), The Lost Road and Other Writings, "Part One: III. The Lost Road, (ii) The Númenórean chapters", pp. 59-61

Tolkien eventually abandoned his work The Lost Road, yet many elements of Herendil were merged into the character of Isildur within The Lord of the Rings.
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), The Lost Road and Other Writings, "Part One: III. The Lost Road, (ii) The Númenórean chapters", p. 70, note 5

claims.text: Herubrand was presumably one of the Riders of Rohan who rode with their King Théoden from Rohan to Gondor. He fought and died in the Battle of the Pelennor Fields on 15 March, . His name is remembered in the poem Song of the Mounds of Mundburg.
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, The Lord of the Rings, The Return of the King, "The Battle of the Pelennor Fields", p. 849; J.R.R. Tolkien, The Lord of the Rings, Appendix B, "The Great Years", entry for the year 3019, March 15, p. 1094

claims.text:
Herucalmo is a Quenya name. As Paul Strack suggests it seems to be a combination of heru ("lord"), cala ("light") with the masculine agentive suffix -mo.
Anducal is a Quenya name. Its meaning is not glossed, but Paul Strack suggests that it perhaps means "Light of the West" as a combination of andu ("west") and cala ("light"). Like all the rulers of Númenor who took their royal names in Quenya, Anducal added the prefix tar- ("high") to his name when he received the Sceptre.
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), Unfinished Tales, "The Line of Elros: Kings of Númenor", first paragraph and entry I to XXV

claims.text: Herucalmo was a descendant of Tar-Atanamir and married Tar-Vanimeldë, the daughter of Tar-Telemmaitë and an older relative and descendant of the same degree from Tar-Atanamir. Together they had a son, Alcarin. Tar-Vanimeldë had little interest in her duties as a ruler (preferring to indulge in music and dance) so Herucalmo wielded the power of the Sceptre of Númenor. When his wife died, Herucalmo usurped the kingship that should have passed on to their son, and ruled Númenor for twenty years until he died in .
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), Unfinished Tales, "The Line of Elros: Kings of Númenor", entry XVI Tar-Vanimeldë

claims.text: Upon his death the Kingship reverted to the rightful heir, Tar-Alcarin.
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), Unfinished Tales, "The Line of Elros: Kings of Númenor", entry XVI Tar-Vanimeldë

claims.text: "Tar-Anducal" being an usurper was not reckoned in the Line of Kings as the seventeenth ruler of Númenor.

claims.text: Hirgon was a grey-eyed tall man. When Merry first saw him he thought he was Boromir, but then realised that he looked like as if he were one of his kin. claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, The Lord of the Rings, The Return of the King, "The Muster of Rohan", pp. 798-801

claims.text: Hirgon was a mounted messenger that was sent by Steward Denethor from Minas Tirith to King Théoden of Rohan during the War of the Ring, expecting assault from Sauron against Gondor.
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, The Lord of the Rings, The Return of the King, "The Muster of Rohan", pp. 798-801

claims.text: Hirgon arrived with a companion in Dunharrow on 9 March . He introduced himself as an errand-rider of Denethor and presented the Red Arrow to King Théoden and told him that Denethor asked him to send the Rohirrim all of his forces as quickly as possible to Minas Tirith to help to defend it. When asked by Théoden if Denethor knew more than he said in his message, Hirgon said that he could not say what Denethor may know or guess. Théoden promised him to come himself with his troops of six thousand Riders would set out for Minas Tirith in the morning, and told to stay until the next day to witness the muster of the troops of Rohan, but that they would not reach Minas Tirith for a week. After witnessing the muster and discussing the necessary provisions for the Rohirrim for their ride, Hirgon and his companion rode back to Gondor on the next day.
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, The Lord of the Rings, Appendix B, "The Great Years", entry for the year 3019, March 9, p. 1093; J.R.R. Tolkien, The Lord of the Rings, The Return of the King, "The Muster of Rohan", pp. 798-801

claims.text: However on their way back they found their deaths. Reached the Rammas Echor, they could not pass through it to reach their city, perhaps because of hostile forces; the two turned back westwards when they were killed between the Grey Wood and the Rammas Echor. His head was hewn off, still clutching the Red Arrow.
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, The Lord of the Rings, The Return of the King, "The Ride of the Rohirrim", p. 835

claims.text: On 14 March the riders of Rohan reached the Grey Wood and camped there. Elfhelm reported to Théoden that scouts found two Gondorian dead messengers and two dead horses between the Grey Wood and the Rammas Echor, and that maybe one of them was Hirgon, because the corpse's head had been hewn off, but the Red Arrow was still held in his hand. They found signs that indicated that the two message riders of Gondor were riding back westwards when they were killed; in the opinion of Elfhelm the two message riders of Gondor reached the Rammas two days earlier (supposing they obtained fresh horses from the posts as message riders usually did), but that they could not pass through it to reach Minas Tirith, because it had either already been taken by or was already under attack by the forces of Sauron and that the two riders had turned back westwards. As a result Théoden concluded that Denethor had not received his message that the Riders of Rohan were coming and would despair that the Rohirrim would not come to help Minas Tirith.
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, The Lord of the Rings, Appendix B, "The Great Years", entry for the year 3019, March 14, p. 1093; J.R.R. Tolkien, The Lord of the Rings, The Return of the King, "The Ride of the Rohirrim", p. 835

claims.text:
In the first very rough draft version of the chapter The Muster of Rohan the messenger that was sent by Denethor to Théoden is briefly mentioned as "Halbarad sister-son of Denethor". In that draft it is not mentioned that he introduced himself to Théoden or that he is questioned by Théoden if Denethor knew more than he said. It is possible that J.R.R. Tolkien abandoned the idea that the messenger was the son of the sister of Denethor, because it is not mentioned in the subsequent versions and he simply introduces himself as an errand-rider of Denethor and responds to Théoden's question that he cannot say what Denethor may know or guess in the published version.
In The Lord of the Rings drafts from the 1940s, this character was first named Dirgon.
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), The War of the Ring, (ii) The Muster of Rohan, original draft 'A', p. 236; J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), The War of the Ring, "Part Three: Minas Tirith", "V. Many Roads lead Eastward (2)", p. 316

claims.text: Hunthor and Dorlas went with Túrin to Nen Girith, where Túrin revealed his plan to climb down the Ravines of Taeglin, cross the river, and ascend the other side so as to strike Glaurung's belly as he stretched across the gap. Dorlas, who had deprecated the other Men of Brethil for lacking courage, could not bring himself to attempt to cross the rock-filled waters. Thus, only Túrin and Hunthor clambered up the west side of the ravine to make their attack.
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), The Children of Húrin, "The Coming of Glaurung"

claims.text: Túrin and Hunthor were nearing the belly of the beast when the heat and stench of the dragon nearly caused Túrin to fall into the river, but Hunthor seized him and saved his life. Túrin proclaimed Hunthor to be of "Great Heart!" but even at the moment a stone struck Hunthor's head and he was lost in the Taeglin.
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), The Children of Húrin, "The Death of Glaurung"

claims.text:
In The Quenta, when Turambar seeks to confront Glómund, he is initially joined by six of his boldest men, but in the night they all slunk away in fear at the rumour of the dragon's arrival, leaving Turambar to confront it alone. In one earlier version of The Grey Annals, Albarth, changed from Albard, was one of Túrin's six companions along with Dorlas. After crossing the Taiglin, Túrin noted that three of his companions were missing and was informed that Albarth fell and was swept away by the Taiglin, while the other two had likely been daunted and slunk away. After emending the tale closer to the final version, where Albarth becomes the one companion who remains with Túrin, his name is changed to Torbarth before becoming Hunthor; in one instance, however, Torbarth was pencilled over with Gwerin.
Gwerin is an early Noldorin name (precursor of Sindarin cerin) meaning "enclosure". In his initial genealogy, Hunthor was the son of Hundad and brother of Harathor (Hardang).

claims.text: In The Quenta, when Turambar seeks to confront Glómund, he is initially joined by six of his boldest men, but in the night they all slunk away in fear at the rumour of the dragon's arrival, leaving Turambar to confront it alone. In one earlier version of The Grey Annals, Albarth, changed from Albard, was one of Túrin's six companions along with Dorlas. After crossing the Taiglin, Túrin noted that three of his companions were missing and was informed that Albarth fell and was swept away by the Taiglin, while the other two had likely been daunted and slunk away. After emending the tale closer to the final version, where Albarth becomes the one companion who remains with Túrin, his name is changed to Torbarth before becoming Hunthor; in one instance, however, Torbarth was pencilled over with Gwerin.

claims.text: Huor was the tallest of all the Edain save his own son Tuor only, and a swift runner. He was noted as wielding an axe. He was likely golden-haired and blue-eyed, as were many of the people of Hador.
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), Unfinished Tales, "Narn i Hîn Húrin (The Tale of the Children of Húrin)", "The Childhood of Túrin"; J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), Unfinished Tales, "Of Tuor and his Coming to Gondolin"; J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), The War of the Jewels, "Part Two. The Later Quenta Silmarillion: Of the Coming of Men into the West (Chapter 14)", p. §33

claims.text:
The name Huor was adapted to Sindarin from the language of the Edain.
In the Etymologies, Noldorin Huor ("'heart-vigour', courage") derives from Common Eldarin Khō-gorē (root KHŌ-N- "heart (physical)"). The Quenya version of Huor is said to be Huore. In the context of this etymology, it has been suggested that Huor can be analyzed as hûr ("vigour, fiery spirit") + a derivative of root GOR ("violence, impetus, haste").
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), The Peoples of Middle-earth, "XI. The Shibboleth of Fëanor", pp. 348, 364 (note 49); J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), The Lost Road and Other Writings, Part Three: "The Etymologies", p. 364; J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), The Lost Road and Other Writings, Part Three: "The Etymologies", p. 359 (entry GOR-)

claims.text: Taller than all Edain but Tuor
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), Unfinished Tales, "Narn i Hîn Húrin (The Tale of the Children of Húrin)"

claims.text: In Morgoth unleashed a terrible assault wherein Galdor's father perished and Galdor thus became the Lord of Dor-lómin. Shortly after this Fingolfin, High King of the Noldor, fell in a duel with Morgoth himself. With the Siege of Angband broken, Orcs began harrying the northern borders of Brethil and Húrin and Huor, who would not be restrained, often went to battle with the Men of Brethil against them.
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), The War of the Jewels, "Part One. The Grey Annals": §147; J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), The Children of Húrin, "The Childhood of Túrin"
claims.section: section == History == > An end of peace and mirth

claims.text: Turgon, the King of Gondolin and son of Fingolfin, welcomed the brothers. Their ancestor Hador was an Elf-friend, and Turgon had been counselled by Ulmo to deal kindly with his house as from them great help would come to him in time of need. Húrin and Huor thus dwelt as guests in Gondolin for nearly a year and Turgon spoke often with the brothers, developing a great liking for them. He thus wished to keep them in Gondolin for both love as well as law, for it was the law of the king that no one who entered Gondolin was able to leave unless the king himself permitted it.
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), The Children of Húrin, "The Childhood of Túrin"
claims.section: section == History == > An end of peace and mirth

claims.text: But Húrin and Huor, with their time of hope and strength as Men being much shorter than that of Elves, desired to return to their people and share in their wars and griefs. They further argued that they knew not the way to Gondolin, being brought by air and their eyes by mercy being veiled. Turgon grieved at this, but relented and gave them permission to leave as they came, if the Eagles were willing.
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), The Children of Húrin, "The Childhood of Túrin"
claims.section: section == History == > An end of peace and mirth

claims.text: The Eagles then carried the brothers off at night, and set them down in Dor-lómin by dawn of the next day. Their kinsfolk rejoiced, as it was believed that they had been captured or slain, but the brothers would speak only that they had been rescued by the Eagles who had brought them home. When questioned by Galdor, who noted that they "found food and fine raiment, and return as young princes, not as waifs of the wood" Húrin shared further only that their return was permitted through an oath of silence, which they were still under. While Galdor did not press the matter, he and many others guessed at the truth, for both the Eagles and the oath pointed to Turgon. The strange fortune of the brothers, and their rumoured friendship with Turgon, became widely known, and reached the ears of the servants of Morgoth.
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), The Children of Húrin, "The Childhood of Túrin"; J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), The War of the Jewels, "Part One. The Grey Annals": §166
claims.section: section == History == > An end of peace and mirth

claims.text: Huor was born in , as the second son of Galdor and therefore of the House of Hador which ruled the realm of Dor-lómin as vassals under the House of Fingolfin. Huor was also closely akin to the House of Haleth through his mother Hareth, and his uncle Haldir who was both the brother of Hareth and husband of Galdor's sister Glóredhel.
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), The War of the Jewels, "Part One. The Grey Annals": §143

claims.text: Huor's elder brother was Húrin, and there was great love between them and they were seldom apart in their youth. At some point in their youth they were sent to Brethil to dwell as foster sons of Haldir, as was the custom among northern Men in those days.
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), The Children of Húrin, "The Childhood of Túrin"

claims.text: In Morgoth renewed his assault and threw a great force against King Fingon in Hithlum. The Orcs won many of the passes, besieged Fingon's fortress of Eithel Sirion, and even came into Mithrim. Galdor, serving as captain at Eithel Sirion in Fingon's stead, was slain by an arrow and Húrin then took up his lordship and command, with "a fire in him that made the sword hot in his hand". Behind Fingon and Hürin the Orcs were driven with great slaughter from the land, and pursued far even into Anfauglith.
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), The War of the Jewels, "Part One. The Grey Annals": §171; J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), The Children of Húrin, "The Childhood of Túrin"; J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), The Lost Road and Other Writings, "Part Two: Valinor and Middle-earth before The Lord of the Rings, VI. Quenta Silmarillion", p. §156; J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), The Lost Road and Other Writings, "Part Two: Valinor and Middle-earth before The Lord of the Rings, VI. Quenta Silmarillion"
claims.section: section == History == > Last days of the House of Hador

claims.text: In , during the first days of spring, Huor wedded Rían, the daughter of Belegund of the House of Bëor, and they soon conceived a son who Huor named "Tuor" even before his birth. Two months following their wedding the summons came for the mustering of the hosts, and Huor and Húrin marched away in the army of Fingon.
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), The War of the Jewels, "Part One. The Grey Annals": §218
claims.section: section == History == > Last days of the House of Hador

claims.text: The day of battle was decided to be the morning of Midsummer, and on that day came forces from many realms and lords. Within Fingon's assembled host, the Men of Dor-lómin under Húrin and Huor were placed on the right, joined by Men of Brethil under their uncle Haldir. Unlooked for, Turgon also arrived, having opened his leaguer to fight alongside his brother Fingon.
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), The Children of Húrin, "The Battle of Unnumbered Tears"
claims.section: section == History == > Last days of the House of Hador

claims.text: The ensuing battle, however, proved disastrous, and in the days that followed Morgoth's forces broke those of the Elves and Men that opposed him. Húrin and Huor, leading the remnant of the House of Hador, stood with Turgon and urged that he withdraw; as the last of the House of Fingolfin, in him lay the last hope of Eldar. Huor further prophesied, with the eyes of death, that from he and Turgon "a new star shall arise". Maeglin, who stood with Turgon, heard these words and did not forget them.
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), The Children of Húrin, "The Battle of Unnumbered Tears"
claims.section: section == History == > Last days of the House of Hador

claims.text: As Turgon withdrew the Men of Dor-lómin provided rearguard, as desired by Húrin and Huor. They did not wish to escape from their lands, and if they could not win back their homes, they would stand to the end. After Turgon passed through the guard of Húrin and Huor, he passed down the Sirion and escaped. Húrin and Huor, however, drew what remained of the House of Hador and, foot by foot withdrew until they passed behind the Fen of Serech and held the stream of Rivil in front of them. There the hosts of Angband were slain in numbers such that they bridged the stream with their dead, but yet they managed to cross and encircle the Men of Dor-lómin. As the sun set, Huor was slain by a venomed arrow to the eye, while his men were slain about him. The Orcs then hewed off their heads and piled them as a mound of gold. Huor's remains were after likely taken and piled into the Hill of the Slain.
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), The Children of Húrin, "The Battle of Unnumbered Tears"; J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), Unfinished Tales, "Of Tuor and his Coming to Gondolin"
claims.section: section == History == > Last days of the House of Hador

claims.text: Húrin is Sindarin, but it is never glossed. However, in the earlier Noldorin phase of the language, the name is the combination of hûr ("vigour") + ind ("heart").
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), The Lost Road and Other Writings, Part Three: "The Etymologies", entries"ID", "KHOR"

claims.text: Blue
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), Unfinished Tales, "Narn i Hîn Húrin (The Tale of the Children of Húrin)"; J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), The Children of Húrin, "The Death of Túrin", p. 255

claims.text: In , the alliance known as Union of Maedhros led Elves, Dwarves, and Men to assault Angband. Húrin led his folk to join the host led by the High King Fingon. In the battle, later named the Nirnaeth Arnoediad or Battle of Unnumbered Tears, the Union were defeated by the hosts of Morgoth. Many Elves and Men perished, including Fingon who was slain by a Balrog. With their liege lord slain and facing a rout, Húrin and Huor convinced Turgon to withdraw and keep the secret of Gondolin. To defend his escape, the Men of Dor-lómin formed a rearguard near the Pass of Sirion and held it giving as much time for Turgon to gather the remainder of Fingon's people and the host of Gondolin to escape. The location of Gondolin remained secret but for the Men of the Dor-lómin this was their last stand for they would not forsake the Northlands and were slaughtered by the hosts of Morgoth. By the Fen of Serech, Huor was slain by an arrow through the eye, but Húrin remained steadfast crying Aurë entuluva!(S) for each foe he slew with his axe, seventy times in all. He fought until he was buried under the weight of bodies of his enemies, then Gothmog bound him and dragged him towards Angband.
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), The Silmarillion, "Quenta Silmarillion: Of the Fifth Battle: Nirnaeth Arnoediad"

claims.text: After the death of his children Morgoth released Húrin, where he hoped he could further his malice. The broken man first returned to Hithlum, which was now ruled by Easterlings. Finding none of his kin, he travelled with outlaws to the mountains of Echoriath, searching for the entrance to Gondolin. At first Turgon refused him, but later recanted and sent Eagles to bring him to Gondolin. Húrin had already left for the Forest of Brethil, but Morgoth's curse had already ensnared Gondolin, for the Dark Lord's spies now knew the general location of the Hidden Kingdom.
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), The Silmarillion, "Quenta Silmarillion: Of the Ruin of Doriath"

claims.text: Húrin continued on to the ruins of Nargothrond; beyond seeking for news and plunder, he had been an admirer of Finrod. In the ruins he found the Petty-dwarf Mîm. The petty-dwarf had betrayed Túrin years ago and in revenge Húrin slaughtered him. Mîm had claimed the treasure of Nargothrond, but Húrin recovered the Nauglamír and journeyed eastwards.
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), The War of the Jewels, "Part Three. The Wanderings of Húrin and Other Writings not forming part of the Quenta Silmarillion: I. The Wanderings of Húrin"; J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), The Silmarillion, "Quenta Silmarillion: Of the Ruin of Doriath"

claims.text: Húrin reached the Meres of Twilight and was taken by the Elves who guarded the western borders of Doriath in . He was allowed to enter Menegroth, where in anger he threw the Nauglamír before King Thingol and 'thanked' him for aiding his son. Thingol's wife, Melian, finally pierced through Húrin's madness and grief revealing the truth that Morgoth hid. Shamed by his actions, he picked up the Nauglamír to give to the king as a gift and memorial, then he left Menegroth no longer a thrall of Morgoth.
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), The War of the Jewels, "Part Three. The Wanderings of Húrin and Other Writings not forming part of the Quenta Silmarillion: I. The Wanderings of Húrin", p. 258; J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), The Silmarillion, "Quenta Silmarillion: Of the Ruin of Doriath"

claims.text: After leaving Menegroth, it is said Húrin, "bereft of all purpose and desire", cast himself into the Great Sea.
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), The Silmarillion, "Quenta Silmarillion: Of the Ruin of Doriath"; J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), The Shaping of Middle-earth, "III. The Quenta: [Section] 14", p. 96:"… it is not said that [Húrin] found [Morwen] ever upon the earth; and some have said that he cast himself at last into the western sea…"

claims.text:
Thalion is simply Sindarin for "Steadfast, Strong".
When Túrin dwelt in Nargothrond, Húrin was indirectly called by him Úmarth, meaning "Ill-fate".
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), The Silmarillion, "Appendix: Elements in Quenya and Sindarin Names", entry thalion; J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), The Children of Húrin, "Túrin in Nargothrond", p. 159; J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), The Silmarillion, "Appendix: Elements in Quenya and Sindarin Names", entry amarth

claims.text: In The Book of Lost Tales, Úrin the Steadfast was a lord of Men who resided in the woodlands. He had a wife, Mavwin and a son, Túrin. Different from many of his folk, he had been a friend of the Elves, most especially the Gnome Egnor, an Elf of the greenwood and renown huntsman. He also knew Beren, son of Egnor, and had once rendered him service in respect of Damrod, son of Beren. He was said to have "marched with countless battalions" alongside Egnor, and been as a brother in arms to Egnor which was emended to him being a brother in arms to Beren.
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), The Book of Lost Tales Part Two, "II. Turambar and the Foalókë"; J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), The Book of Lost Tales Part One, "X. Gilfanon's Tale: The Travail of the Noldoli and the Coming of Mankind"; J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), The Book of Lost Tales Part Two, "I. The Tale of Tinúviel": "The second version of the Tale of Tinúviel"
claims.section: section == Other versions of the legendarium == > Book of Lost Tales

claims.text: Úrin hearkened to the summons of the Gnomes and with his folk marched with the Ilkorindi against Melko. In the ensuing Battle of Lamentation the people of Úrin were among the few kindreds of Men who did not flee from battle, and were instead slain except for Úrin who was made captive.
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), The Book of Lost Tales Part Two, "II. Turambar and the Foalókë"
claims.section: section == Other versions of the legendarium == > Book of Lost Tales

claims.text: Melko then attempted to constrain Úrin to take up his employ, and seek after Turgon as a spy. However, neither threats of torture nor promises of riches would cause Úrin to yield. In anger, Melko then cursed a doom of woe upon Úrin and his folk, magically bound Úrin to a lofty place in the mountains, and gave Úrin a measure of vision by which he might see those things which befell his wife and children and be powerless to aid. After Melko gloated that “the life of Túrin thy son shall be accounted a matter for tears wherever Elves or Men are gathered for the telling of tales”, Úrin replied that “At least none shall pity him for this, that he had a craven for father.” Shortly after, Mavwin gave birth to their daughter, Nienóri, and sent Túrin to foster with Tinwelint. Due to the renown of Úrin, and his bond with Beren, Tinwelint accepted Túrin not as a retainer, but as even a second child.
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), The Book of Lost Tales Part Two, "II. Turambar and the Foalókë"
claims.section: section == Other versions of the legendarium == > Book of Lost Tales

claims.text: As the years passed, the dread happenings of Mavwin, Túrin, and Nienóri were witnessed by Úrin, and though Melko continually tempted him to yield, Úrin refused. However, after the deaths of Túrin, and Nienóri, the doom of Úrin's folk had been utterly fulfilled and Melko thought to use him in a more subtle way. Melko put evil words of distrust to Úrin, and then released him.
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), The Book of Lost Tales Part Two, "II. Turambar and the Foalókë"
claims.section: section == Other versions of the legendarium == > Book of Lost Tales

claims.text: Úrin, bowed with years and sorrow, and bitter in spirit, then departed unmolested from Melko's lands. Around himself he gathered a band of exiled wild Elves who were fierce and lawless. These he led to the caves of the Rodothlim where they encountered Mîm the Dwarf and the cursed gold. Though Mîm warned them not to touch the treasure, Úrin's outlaws made to carry it off regardless. When Mîm then began cursing them for doing so, Úrin smote the Dwarf, and Mîm then lay one final curse upon the gold before his death.
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), The Book of Lost Tales Part Two, "II. Turambar and the Foalókë"
claims.section: section == Other versions of the legendarium == > Book of Lost Tales

claims.text: Úrin then ordered his outlaws to carry the gold to the halls of Tinwelint. They murmured against doing so, but Úrin responded that Tinwelint, that "king of greed", would reward them with a much sweeter life for the treasure than all the gold in Valinor could get them out in the empty woods. The hoard was then arranged for transport, placed in sacks or shut in boxes of rough wood, and so great was it that Úrin's company could scarce bear it. Úrin eventually brought it to Tinwelint's hall, and there he was greeted with joy and amazement. Úrin rebuked this welcome though, and fiercely told Tinwelint and his court of the unfortunate fates of Túrin and Nienóri. He then revealed the vast treasure, mockingly gifted it to Tinwelint as payment in full his services, and insulted him. At this Tinwelint lost his patience, and chastised Úrin and ordered him to be gone. He would not, however, have Úrin slain out of remembrance for his greet deeds of valiance.
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), The Book of Lost Tales Part Two, "II. Turambar and the Foalókë"
claims.section: section == Other versions of the legendarium == > Book of Lost Tales

claims.text: Úrin departed and returned to Hisilómë where he died among Men. However, it was said that in death his shade fared into the woods seeking Mavwin, and the two then haunted the woods about the fall of Silver Bowl, where their children had perished, bewailing them. The Elves of Kôr], however, further tell that Úrin and Mavwin eventually fared to Mandos, and there they prayed to Manwë so that the Gods would have mercy on the unhappy fate of Túrin and Ninóri.
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), The Book of Lost Tales Part Two, "II. Turambar and the Foalókë"
claims.section: section == Other versions of the legendarium == > Book of Lost Tales

claims.text: For the meaning of his name refer to Húrin of Emyn Arnen - Etymology. Húrin I was probably named after Húrin Thalion, the last Lord of Dor-lómin and one of the great heroes of the Edain in the First Age of the House of Hador, from which the Kings of Gondor were descended on the male side.
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, Carl F. Hostetter (ed.), "Part Two. Body, Mind and Spirit: V. Beards", The Nature of Middle-earth, HarperCollins, 2021, footnote 3, p. 189; J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), The Peoples of Middle-earth, "VII. The Heirs of Elendil", The Ruling Stewards of Gondor, p. 203

claims.text: Húrin became the fifth Ruling Steward at the death of his father, Steward Belegorn in .
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, The Lord of the Rings, Appendix A, "The Númenorean Kings", "The Realms in Exile", "The Southern Line: Heirs of Anarion", Ruling Stewards, entry for Belegorn, p. 1039

claims.text: Húrin's rule was a quiet time for Gondor during the Watchful Peace, when Sauron was in the East and the Nazgûl stayed quiet in Minas Morgul.
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, The Lord of the Rings, Appendix A, "The Númenorean Kings", "Gondor and the Heirs of Anárion", "The Stewards", fourth paragraph, p. 1053; J.R.R. Tolkien, The Lord of the Rings, Appendix B, "The Third Age", entries for the years 2063 and 2460, p. 1087

claims.text: Húrin ruled as Steward for forty years, and was succeeded by his son, Túrin I..
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, The Lord of the Rings, Appendix A, "The Númenorean Kings", "The Realms in Exile", "The Southern Line: Heirs of Anarion", Ruling Stewards, entry for Húrin I, p. 1039; J.R.R. Tolkien, The Lord of the Rings, Appendix A, "The Númenorean Kings", "The Realms in Exile", "The Southern Line: Heirs of Anarion", Ruling Stewards, entry for Túrin I, p. 1039

claims.text: For the meaning of his name refer to Húrin of Emyn Arnen - Etymology. Húrin II was probably named after the hero of the First Age Húrin Thalion, the Lord of Dor-lómin.
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, Carl F. Hostetter (ed.), "Part Two. Body, Mind and Spirit: V. Beards", The Nature of Middle-earth, HarperCollins, 2021, footnote 3, p. 189; J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), The Peoples of Middle-earth, "VII. The Heirs of Elendil", p. 203

claims.text: Húrin ruled Gondor as its Steward for twenty-three years, and was succeeded by his son, Belecthor I.
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, The Lord of the Rings, Appendix A, "The Númenorean Kings", "The Realms in Exile", "The Southern Line: Heirs of Anarion"

claims.text: Húrin is a Sindarin name. Its meaning is not glossed, but the Association Tollkiendil suggests it means "Strong Heart". It is probably a combination of hûr ("vigour", "fiery spirit", readiness for action) and ind ("heart"). Húrin of Emyn Arnen was named after the hero of the First Age Húrin Thalion.
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, Carl F. Hostetter (ed.), "Part Two. Body, Mind and Spirit: V. Beards", The Nature of Middle-earth, HarperCollins, 2021, footnote 3, p. 189
claims.finding_aid: Tolkien Gateway, “Húrin of Emyn Arnen”, revid 414927 (2024-12-13T01:35:36Z)

claims.text: Being a noble of high trust and wisdom (and of ultimately royal descent, being a kinsman of King Minardil), he was chosen to serve under the King as Steward of Gondor.
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, Carl F. Hostetter (ed.), "Part Two. Body, Mind and Spirit: V. Beards", The Nature of Middle-earth, HarperCollins, 2021, p. 188; J.R.R. Tolkien, The Lord of the Rings, Appendix A, "The Númenorean Kings", "Gondor and the Heirs of Anárion", "The Stewards"
claims.finding_aid: Tolkien Gateway, “Húrin of Emyn Arnen”, revid 414927 (2024-12-13T01:35:36Z)

claims.text: However, unlike any previous stewards, whose chief task was the supervision of the King's estates and properties, Húrin acted as the chief counsellor to the King, as well as being granted the right to assume the duties of the King in his absence, and having a say in choosing a successor to the throne, in the case the King died without an apparent heir.
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, Carl F. Hostetter (ed.), "Part Two. Body, Mind and Spirit: V. Beards", The Nature of Middle-earth, HarperCollins, 2021, p. 188
claims.finding_aid: Tolkien Gateway, “Húrin of Emyn Arnen”, revid 414927 (2024-12-13T01:35:36Z)

claims.text: During his service, Húrin laboured greatly on the ordering of Gondor in the days of the Great Plague.
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), The Peoples of Middle-earth, "VII. The Heirs of Elendil"
claims.finding_aid: Tolkien Gateway, “Húrin of Emyn Arnen”, revid 414927 (2024-12-13T01:35:36Z)

claims.text: Afterwards, Minardil's heirs opted to select their own Stewards not from any noble Gondorians, but from Húrin's sons and descendants; thus Stewardship was connected to the House of Húrin, and after some generations it became hereditary.
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, The Lord of the Rings, Appendix A, "The Númenorean Kings", "Gondor and the Heirs of Anárion", "The Stewards"
claims.finding_aid: Tolkien Gateway, “Húrin of Emyn Arnen”, revid 414927 (2024-12-13T01:35:36Z)

claims.text: Húrin fought in the Battle of the Pelennor Fields, during which the Rohirrim were outnumbered and hard-pressed. Húrin, along with Forlong, Hirluin, and Imrahil came to their aid.
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, The Lord of the Rings, The Return of the King, "The Battle of the Pelennor Fields"
claims.finding_aid: Tolkien Gateway, “Húrin (Warden of the Keys)”, revid 396218 (2024-06-25T19:37:30Z)

claims.text: A barricade was laid in place of the destroyed Great Gate at the gatehouse of the city. After the Fall of Sauron, at the coronation of Aragorn, he ceremoniously opened that barricade for the entry of the new king.
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, The Lord of the Rings, The Return of the King, "The Steward and the King"

claims.text:
Ciryaher is a name Quenya. Its meaning is not glossed, but as Paul Strack explains, it probably means "Ship Lord" and be a compound of cirya ("ship") and heru ("lord").
Hyarmendacil is Quenya. It means "South-victor". It is a compound of hyarmen ("south") and -(n)dacil ("victor").
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, The Lord of the Rings, Appendix A, "The Númenorean Kings", "Gondor and the Heirs of Anárion", entry for king Ciryaher

claims.text: Ciryaher was the son of King Ciryandil, one of the Ship-kings.
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, The Lord of the Rings, Appendix A, "The Númenorean Kings", "Gondor and the Heirs of Anárion", entry for king Ciryaher

claims.text: Ciryaher ascended the throne after his father Ciryandil was slain during a siege of Umbar in by the Haradrim, which were led by lords that had been driven from Umbar after it had been conquered by his grandfather Eärnil I. The siege of Umbar lasted for many years, but the Haradrim could not take Umbar, because of the power of the ships of Gondor.
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, The Lord of the Rings, Appendix B, "The Third Age", entry for the year 1015; J.R.R. Tolkien, The Lord of the Rings, Appendix A, "The Númenorean Kings", "Gondor and the Heirs of Anárion", entry for king Eärnil I and for king Ciryandil; J.R.R. Tolkien, The Lord of the Rings, Appendix A, "The Númenorean Kings", "Gondor and the Heirs of Anárion", entry for king Ciryaher

claims.text: Ciryaher began his reign by building up Gondor's army and navy, When he had assembled enough forces, Ciryaher came from Gondor by sea and by land. His armies crossed the river Harnen and completely defeated the Haradrim. The kings of the Men of Harad were forced to acknowledge the overlordship of Gondor in and their sons lived as hostages in the court of the King of Gondor. After this victory he took the name Hyarmendacil, which means "South-victor".
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, The Lord of the Rings, Appendix A, "The Númenorean Kings", "Gondor and the Heirs of Anárion", entry for king Ciryaher

claims.text: During his reign Gondor reached its greatest extent and power. Gondor extended north to the Field of Celebrant and to the southern end of Mirkwood, west to the river Greyflood, east to the inland Sea of Rhûn, south to the river Harnen and along the coast to the peninsula and haven of Umbar. The Men of the Vales of Anduin acknowledged the authority of Gondor. For the rest of his reign Gondor was at peace, because no enemies dared to attack Gondor. The watch on Mordor was maintained through great fortresses that guaraded the passes to Mordor.
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, The Lord of the Rings, Appendix A, "The Númenorean Kings", "Gondor and the Heirs of Anárion", entry for king Ciryaher

claims.text: Hyarmendacil reigned for one hundred and thirty-four years, which was the longest reign of all the Kings of Gondor of the line of Anárion, except one. He was the last of the Ship-kings and was succeeded by his lazy son Atanatar II Alcarin.
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, The Lord of the Rings, Appendix A, "The Númenorean Kings", "Gondor and the Heirs of Anárion", entry for king Ciryaher; J.R.R. Tolkien, The Lord of the Rings, Appendix A, "The Númenorean Kings", "Gondor and the Heirs of Anárion", entry for king Atanatar Alcarin

claims.text:
A late manuscript of what would later become Appendix A also mentioned that after his victory over the kings of Harad, Gondor occupied all the land south of the mouths of the river Anduin up to the river Harnen and the borders of Near Harad and all the coastland as far as Umbar. It also mentions that Umbar became a great fortress and haven for the ships of Gondor and that only king Tarondor reigned longer than Hyarmendacil.

claims.text: Ibun lived with his family at Amon Rûdh. They were seen by the Gaurwaith as they snuck past them carrying heavy sacks. Mîm was captured, and the two brothers fled into the mist. As they ran, Khîm was shot by a wild arrow from the outlaws, but Ibun survived, and shared his father's House of Ransom with Túrin and the outlaws.
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), The Children of Húrin, "Of Mîm the Dwarf", p. 132

claims.text: One winter, the two Petty-dwarves went out in search of roots, and were captured by a band of Orcs. To save his life Mîm betrayed Túrin to the Orcs, but Ibun's fate is unclear.
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), The Children of Húrin, "The Land of Bow and Helm", p. 148

claims.text: Much later, in Nargothrond, Mîm told Húrin, "I am the last of my people", meaning that he outlived both his sons; Ibun either lost his life at the hands of the Orcs, or in some later unrecorded mishap.
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), The Silmarillion, "Quenta Silmarillion: Of the Ruin of Doriath"

claims.text: Christopher Tolkien has noted that Idis is similar to the Old English poetic word ides ("woman, lady").
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), The Treason of Isengard, "XXVI. The King of the Golden Hall", Notes, note 15, p. 450

claims.text: Idis first appeared alongside Éowyn assisting Théoden in Meduseld after Gandalf's triumph against Wormtongue. When Aragorn first saw Éowyn in daylight, she was described as being younger than Idis. Later, when Gandalf asks Théoden who will lead Rohan when they depart to war, Théoden chooses Éowyn, his niece, and not Idis, his daughter; despite Idis being present at that very moment. At the meal before Théoden and his Men depart to war, Idis is not mentioned as Éowyn alone brought wine to the meal. At the same meal, Háma tells Théoden that the House of Eorl would not die with Éomer, as Idis was Théoden's daughter and Éowyn was Éomer's sister. Háma then stated that "All love her. Let her be as lord to the Eorlingas, while we are gone", indicating Éowyn, and Éowyn alone, with Idis never appearing again.
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), The Treason of Isengard, "XXVI. The King of the Golden Hall", pp. 445, 447

claims.text: In a very early draft, Idis was originally named Ælflæd, which Christopher Tolkien notes was struck out soon after.
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), The Treason of Isengard, "XXVI. The King of the Golden Hall", Notes, note 15, p. 450

claims.text: Tolkien eventually discarded Idis when the story of Éowyn overshadowed her.
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), The Treason of Isengard, "XXVI. The King of the Golden Hall", pp. 445, 447

claims.text:
Idril Celebrindal was the only child of Turgon. She participated in the Flight of the Noldor, and had to cross the Helcaraxë with the host of Fingolfin. She and her mother Elenwë fell into the bitter waters, and Turgon risked his life to save them. But he only could save Idril, and her mother was covered in fallen ice.
200px|left|thumb|Grinding Ice by [[Marya Filatova]]
Together with Orodreth and Celebrimbor, she was one of the three Noldor in the third generation to come into exile. She lived in Vinyamar in the first years after the Flight, but later she moved with her people to the Hidden City of Gondolin between and . In the city, the smithcraft Enerdhil made the famous gem Elessar, and he gave it to Idril, who wore it upon her breast.
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), The Peoples of Middle-earth, "XI. The Shibboleth of Fëanor", "The names of Finwë's descendants", pp. 343-344; J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), The War of the Jewels, "Part One. The Grey Annals", §§88, 113; J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), Unfinished Tales, "The History of Galadriel and Celeborn", "The Elessar", p. 249

claims.text: Maeglin, the son of Aredhel, Turgon's sister, became interested on Idril even before coming to the city, and when he saw her for the first time "she seemed to him as the sun from which all the King's hall drew its light." She was the only one who could pierce into his mind, and knowing his thought of her she loved him the less, as they were too closely related.
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), The Silmarillion, "Quenta Silmarillion: Of Maeglin"

claims.text: When Tuor son of Huor was received in Gondolin, Idril sat on the left of her father. And while living there, the heart of Idril was turned to Tuor, and his to her. Because Turgon had grown to love Tuor as a son (as he had his father before), and remembering the last words of Huor, he allowed Idril and Tuor to wed, thus bringing about the second union of Elves and Men, after Beren and Lúthien. From them Eärendil Half-elven was born, and she gave him the mother-name Ardamírë, that foretold his destiny.
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), The Silmarillion, "Quenta Silmarillion: Of Tuor and the Fall of Gondolin"; J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), The Peoples of Middle-earth, "XI. The Shibboleth of Fëanor", "The names of Finwë's descendants", p. 348

claims.text: Years later, Morgoth had increased his efforts to find the city, "but Idril Celebrindal was wise and farseeing, and her heart misgave her, and foreboding crept upon her spirit as a cloud." Therefore, Idril let prepare a secret way, and she contrived that this work was not known to Maeglin. Thus, when the Fall of Gondolin began, she and Tuor were able to lead many survivors out of the city and save their lives.
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), The Silmarillion, "Quenta Silmarillion: Of Tuor and the Fall of Gondolin"

claims.text: When Tuor grew old, he departed in his ship Eärrámë for the West, and Idril went with him. Before leaving, she gave the Elessar to her son, saying: "The Elessar I leave with thee, for there are grievous hurts to Middle-earth which thou maybe shalt heal." It is believed by the Elves and Dúnedain that Idril and Tuor arrived in Valinor, and it is said that Tuor became reckoned in the kindred of the Elves, so that they both live in Valinor.
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), Unfinished Tales, "The History of Galadriel and Celeborn", "The Elessar", p. 249; J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), The Silmarillion, "Quenta Silmarillion: Of Tuor and the Fall of Gondolin"

claims.text:
In The Book of Lost Tales, Idril meant "Beloved" in Gnomish, but Elves often called her Idhril, or in Qenya Irildë, which meant "mortal maiden", because she married Tuor. Her after name "Silver Feet" was Tal-Celeb in Gnomish, and Taltelepta in Qenya.
Idril's fate was woven with Tuor's since she first saw him from a high window the day he came to the city. Tuor also loved her in secret for many years until his heart was full, and Turgon did not oppose to their union. This was the first marriage between a Man and an Elf, and it was made in Gar Ainion to the great joy of the Gondothlim, except Meglin.
Idril had great skill to see the hearts of Elves and Men, and a special power to foresee the future. Thus, one year after the birth of Eärendel, she told Tuor of a dream she had: Meglin threw their son into a furnace and he wanted to thrust them in too. Therefore, she asked Tuor to begin the building of a secret way. Seven years later, Idril became taciturn, and prophesied to Tuor that he would have to make a choice, and that the time was near. Her husband could not understand her, but obeyed her counsels.
thumb|right|Action-girl Idril by [[Marya Filatova]]
When the Fall of Gondolin began, she arrayed herself in mail, and gave Eärendel a tiny mail coat she had ordered in secret. But her house was attacked by the folk of the Mole, and Meglin tried to throw Eärendel from the walls while dragging her by the hair to make her see it. But Eärendel resisted and "she fought, alone as she was, like a tigress for all her beauty and slenderness". Then came Tuor and his folk of the Wing, saving them. Her husband left her there with Voronwë and other men, and went to battle.
During the siege of the city, Idril was in the door of her house and sent most of her guard down the secret tunnel with Eärendel. But she refused to leave without her lord. Meanwhile, she gathered women and wanderers, showing them the secret tunnel; and her men helped her fighting marauders, but they might not dissuade her from bearing a sword. However, a band of enemies took over the house, and Idril became distraught by grief and fatigue, and running away from the house she arrived to Gar Ainion. There Tuor found her like in the day of their wedding, but she could not recognize him: she was out of her mind, watching the fall of her father. Then Tuor took her and went down the secret tunnel. When the Exiles of Gondolin reached Tumladin, she spoke against those who wanted to march to the Way of Escape, explaining it was no longer protected, "for what magic stands if Gondolin be fallen?" After the survivors were saved by the Eagles, Idril and her people wore an eagle as emblem.
Tolkien did not finish The Book of Lost Tales, so the end of Idril and Tuor is very different in each outline of their story. Like in the published Silmarillion, in all versions Tuor sails west after falling into age. In the most repeated version, Tuor sails without Idril, who grieves him with Eärendel; later she vanishes (sailing at night). In another version, Idril swam after her husband. In a separate note, Tolkien considered her death, but this contradicts the last one he chose, in which "Tuor and Idril some say sail now in Swanwing and may be seen going swift down the wind at down and dusk".

claims.text: Idril's fate was woven with Tuor's since she first saw him from a high window the day he came to the city. Tuor also loved her in secret for many years until his heart was full, and Turgon did not oppose to their union. This was the first marriage between a Man and an Elf, and it was made in Gar Ainion to the great joy of the Gondothlim, except Meglin.
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), The Book of Lost Tales Part Two, "III. The Fall of Gondolin", p. 164
claims.section: section == Other versions of the legendarium ==

claims.text:
Idril had great skill to see the hearts of Elves and Men, and a special power to foresee the future. Thus, one year after the birth of Eärendel, she told Tuor of a dream she had: Meglin threw their son into a furnace and he wanted to thrust them in too. Therefore, she asked Tuor to begin the building of a secret way. Seven years later, Idril became taciturn, and prophesied to Tuor that he would have to make a choice, and that the time was near. Her husband could not understand her, but obeyed her counsels.
thumb|right|Action-girl Idril by [[Marya Filatova]]
When the Fall of Gondolin began, she arrayed herself in mail, and gave Eärendel a tiny mail coat she had ordered in secret. But her house was attacked by the folk of the Mole, and Meglin tried to throw Eärendel from the walls while dragging her by the hair to make her see it. But Eärendel resisted and "she fought, alone as she was, like a tigress for all her beauty and slenderness". Then came Tuor and his folk of the Wing, saving them. Her husband left her there with Voronwë and other men, and went to battle.
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), The Book of Lost Tales Part Two, "III. The Fall of Gondolin", p. 167–8; J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), The Book of Lost Tales Part Two, "III. The Fall of Gondolin", p. 170–1; J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), The Book of Lost Tales Part Two, "III. The Fall of Gondolin", p. 174; J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), The Book of Lost Tales Part Two, "III. The Fall of Gondolin", p. 177–8
claims.section: section == Other versions of the legendarium ==

claims.text: During the siege of the city, Idril was in the door of her house and sent most of her guard down the secret tunnel with Eärendel. But she refused to leave without her lord. Meanwhile, she gathered women and wanderers, showing them the secret tunnel; and her men helped her fighting marauders, but they might not dissuade her from bearing a sword. However, a band of enemies took over the house, and Idril became distraught by grief and fatigue, and running away from the house she arrived to Gar Ainion. There Tuor found her like in the day of their wedding, but she could not recognize him: she was out of her mind, watching the fall of her father. Then Tuor took her and went down the secret tunnel. When the Exiles of Gondolin reached Tumladin, she spoke against those who wanted to march to the Way of Escape, explaining it was no longer protected, "for what magic stands if Gondolin be fallen?" After the survivors were saved by the Eagles, Idril and her people wore an eagle as emblem.
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), The Book of Lost Tales Part Two, "III. The Fall of Gondolin", p. 186–9; J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), The Book of Lost Tales Part Two, "III. The Fall of Gondolin", p. 193
claims.section: section == Other versions of the legendarium ==

claims.text: Tolkien did not finish The Book of Lost Tales, so the end of Idril and Tuor is very different in each outline of their story. Like in the published Silmarillion, in all versions Tuor sails west after falling into age. In the most repeated version, Tuor sails without Idril, who grieves him with Eärendel; later she vanishes (sailing at night). In another version, Idril swam after her husband. In a separate note, Tolkien considered her death, but this contradicts the last one he chose, in which "Tuor and Idril some say sail now in Swanwing and may be seen going swift down the wind at down and dusk".
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), The Book of Lost Tales Part Two, "V. The Tale of Eärendel", p. 253–4; J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), The Book of Lost Tales Part Two, "V. The Tale of Eärendel", p. 260; J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), The Book of Lost Tales Part Two, "V. The Tale of Eärendel", p. 263; J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), The Book of Lost Tales Part Two, "V. The Tale of Eärendel", p. 255

The meaning of the name Ilberic is unknown. J.R.R. Tolkien noted that the names of the Bucklanders had a vaguely Celtic style.
Jim Allan suggests that the name Ilberic seems to be Germanic. It is a variaton of the name Alberic and contains the elements alb ("Elf") and ric ("reign", "rule"). Alberic is a dwarf king in medieval German heroic literature who appears in Richard Wagner's Ring cycle.
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, The Lord of the Rings, Appendix F, "On Translation", p. 1135

She appears in the Qenyaqetsa, in a rejected early entry. There she is described as:

claims.text:
Imrahil is an Adûnaic name. Its meaning is not glossed.
The second element -hil, also seen in the name Adrahil, is perhaps related to the Westron ending -kil and perhaps ultimately related to Elvish "follower" (KHIL).
Considering the Elvish root KHIL, Carl F. Hostetter and Patrick H. Wynne have proposed as a possible meaning "Heir of Imra" with the first element Imra being the same as the first element in the name Imrazôr and the second element -hil ("heir").
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, The Lord of the Rings, Appendix E, "Pronunciation of Words and Names", "Consonants", entry CH, p. 1113; J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), The Peoples of Middle-earth, "II. The Appendix on Languages", manuscript F2, §9 footnote concerning names in Quenya; J.R.R. claims.text: Imrahil was the only son of Adrahil of Dol Amroth. He had two older sisters, Ivriniel and Finduilas. After his father's death, he became Prince in . Imrahil had four children: Elphir, Erchirion, Amrothos and Lothíriel.
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), The Peoples of Middle-earth, "VII. The Heirs of Elendil", The Line of Dol Amroth, p. 221

claims.text: After the War of the Ring, Prince Imrahil and his nephew Faramir, Prince of Ithilien, were King Elessar's chief commanders. Imrahil was also part of the Great Council of Gondor, and remained an advisor of the King.
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien; Humphrey Carpenter, Christopher Tolkien (eds.), The Letters of J.R.R. Tolkien, Letter 244, (undated, written circa 1963)

claims.text: Prince Imrahil died in the year of the Fourth Age, and was succeed by his eldest son Elphir, who continued the line of Princes.
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), The Peoples of Middle-earth, "VII. The Heirs of Elendil", The Line of Dol Amroth, p. 221

claims.text: Imrahil survived the battle unscathed, and together with Éomer and Aragorn he came to the Great Gate of Minas Tirith. Imrahil recognized that Aragorn was the rightful King, but he agreed that it was wise for Aragorn to wait to enter the city, because he knew Denethor was strong-willed and proud.
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, The Lord of the Rings, The Return of the King, "The Battle of the Pelennor Fields", p. 849
claims.section: section == History == > War of the Ring

claims.text: On 16 March, , Legolas recognized that Imrahil had elven-blood when he looked at him during their meeting in Minas Tirith. On the same day Imrahil participated in the debate of the Captains of the West. Gandalf proposed that they march to the Morannon to distract Sauron's attention from Frodo the Ring-bearer. Aragorn agreed to this advice and said that he did not yet claim to command any man, so the others should choose if they wanted to follow it. Imrahil said that he considered Aragorn to be his liege-lord, regardless whether Aragorn claimed it or not and that he would follow him. Imrahil also stated that he stood in the place of the Steward of Gondor and advised that some troops should remain to protect the City. In the end it was decided that an army of 7,000 would ride forth. Imrahil laughed at the thought. Húrin the Tall was left behind in command.
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, The Lord of the Rings, The Return of the King, "The Last Debate", p. 872; J.R.R. Tolkien, The Lord of the Rings, The Return of the King, "The Last Debate", pp. 878-82
claims.section: section == History == > War of the Ring

claims.text: The Host of the West left Minas Tirith on 18 March. Bypassing Minas Morgul and marching North, the heralds announced the coming of King Elessar at Imrahil's advice. When Sauron's forces emerged from the Black Gate on March 25, Imrahil stood on the front line with his men. They fought the Battle of the Morannon until the One Ring was destroyed.
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, The Lord of the Rings, The Return of the King, "The Black Gate Opens", p. 891
claims.section: section == History == > War of the Ring

claims.text: Prince Imrahil was present at the celebrations of the field of Cormallen, and the coronation of Aragorn as King Elessar, and rode with the funeral procession of King Théoden to Rohan, remaining in Edoras after the King's burial on August 10. Imrahil and Éomer became great friends, and in Éomer wed Imrahil's daughter Lothíriel.
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, The Lord of the Rings, Appendix A, "The House of Eorl", "The Kings of the Mark", Third Line, entry 2991-F.A. 63 Éomer Éadig, p. 1070
claims.section: section == History == > War of the Ring

The first element imra (perhaps from *imar) is not translated but it also appears in the name of his descendant, Imrahil and perhaps Imâr.
Imrazôr, who seems to have retained the usage of Adûnaic in his House, was also known as the Númenórean. Why a Gondorian noble of the Third Age would be called the "Númenórean" is not made clear from the context.

claims.text: Indis was born at Cuiviénen before the Great March of the Eldar to Aman. She was close kin to Ingwë, King of the Vanyar (see below).
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, Carl F. Hostetter (ed.), "Part One. Time and Ageing: XVII. Generational Schemes", The Nature of Middle-earth, HarperCollins, 2021, pp. 127/8 & 142

claims.text: At some point while the Noldor and Vanyar dwelt together in Tirion, her heart turned towards Finwë, though he was wed to Míriel Þerindë. When Ingwë and the Vanyar left Tirion to dwell in the plains of Valinor, Indis accompanied them and stayed near Ingwë's house on the western slopes of Taniquetil. During this time, Indis often wandered the fields of Valinor alone, singing.
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), Morgoth's Ring, "Part Three. The Later Quenta Silmarillion: (II) The Second Phase: Later versions of the Story of Finwë and Míriel", §23-27 pp. 261-2
claims.section: section == History == > Early years in Aman

claims.text: After the birth of Fëanor, Míriel chose to die and refused to be reembodied or healed, leaving her husband Finwë in an unfair widowhood. Ingwë, seeing Finwë's grief, invited him to leave Tirion and dwell in the light of the Trees for a season, to bring him some distance from the memories of his loss. Initially Finwë declined this invitation, but later thought better of it and departed Tirion for the house of Ingwë. In his journey along the paths of the Mountain, Finwë chanced to encounter Indis; in that moment his heart turned towards her, and they recognized their mutual love.
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), Morgoth's Ring, "Part Three. The Later Quenta Silmarillion: (II) The Second Phase: Later versions of the Story of Finwë and Míriel", §23-27 pp. 261-2
claims.section: section == History == > Early years in Aman

claims.text: With the Statute of Finwë and Míriel, Manwë allowed Finwë to take a second wife and Indis thus became the stepmother to Fëanor. Indis bore four children to Finwë: Findis, Fingolfin, Írimë, and Finarfin. Fëanor never became close with his stepmother or half-siblings, and dwelt apart from them as soon as he was of age to do so.
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), Morgoth's Ring, "Part Three. The Later Quenta Silmarillion: (II) The Second Phase: Laws and Customs among the Eldar, [Text A]", pp. 238-9
claims.section: section == History == > Early years in Aman

claims.text: In Melkor destroyed the Two Trees and Darkened Valinor; shortly after he further raided Formenos to steal Fëanor's silmarils and slew Finwë in the process. In the Halls of Mandos Finwë was reacquainted with Míriel, and when she informed him of her desire to live again he pleaded with Vairë to forgo his own return to life in Arda in exchange for Míriel to be reembodied. At this Vairë alleged that in his pity for Míriel, Finwë had forgotten Indis and his children. Finwë responded that his love for each woman did not diminish that for the other, and that he had already been parted from Indis, having not seen her for many years. He further stated that even if he did return, it would be of little comfort to her: her love was most for Fingolfin, and though she may miss his (Fingolfin's) father, she did not miss the father of Fëanor. Further, he stated that above all Indis wished to return to the halls of Ingwë and the peace of the Vanyar. This request was ultimately accepted by Mandos.
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), Morgoth's Ring, "Part Three. The Later Quenta Silmarillion: (II) The Second Phase: Laws and Customs among the Eldar, [Text A]", pp. 252–3
claims.section: section == History == > Following the death of Finwë

claims.text: The last that was known of Indis was that she, along with Findis, did not go into exile, but went to abide among the Vanyar in grief until such time as it seemed good to Manwë to restore Finwë to life.
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), The Peoples of Middle-earth, "XI. The Shibboleth of Fëanor", "The names of Finwë's descendants", p. 343
claims.section: section == History == > Following the death of Finwë

claims.text: The unrest in the House of Finwë – and among the Noldor in general – was exacerbated by a seemingly trivial linguistic matter. The Quenya spoken by all three kindreds of the Eldar at the time of their arrival in Aman included the letter and sound þ. The Vanyar and Falmari retained this, but at some point after the departure of the Vanyar from Tirion, the Noldor had chosen to exchange þ for s in both writing and speech. This change would have turned Míriel's mother-name "Þerindë" into "Serindë," but Míriel herself desired that her name continue to be spoken and written with þ.
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), The Peoples of Middle-earth, "XI. The Shibboleth of Fëanor", "The case of the Quenya change of Þ to s", p. 333-6
claims.section: section == History == > Unrest of the Noldor

claims.text: As long as Míriel lived – and while he retained hope that she might return from death – Finwë himself retained þ in his speech in deference to Míriel. However, after her conclusive refusal to return to life, Finwë also adopted the change to s. By this time, the shift was nearly universal among the Noldor – except by Fëanor, who closely identified þ with his late mother.
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), The Peoples of Middle-earth, "XI. The Shibboleth of Fëanor", "The case of the Quenya change of Þ to s", p. 333-6
claims.section: section == History == > Unrest of the Noldor

claims.text: When Indis wed Finwë, she ceased the use of þ, which was part of her native Vanyarin dialect, and adopted s out of loyalty to her husband and to show her loyalty to her new people, the Noldor. However, Fëanor believed she did so in belittlement of his late mother, and thus made þ into a dire personal and political matter. He demanded that his House and all his true supporters use þ; his opponents (and alienated former supporters) therefore became all the more committed to s. This became yet another source and symptom of unrest among the fractious Noldor.
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), The Peoples of Middle-earth, "XI. The Shibboleth of Fëanor", "The case of the Quenya change of Þ to s", p. 333-6
claims.section: section == History == > Unrest of the Noldor

claims.text: In , tensions between Fëanor and Indis' children boiled over. In a quarrel, Fëanor drew a sword against his eldest half-brother Fingolfin, and for this crime was exiled from Tirion by edict of the Valar. Finwë accompanied his eldest son into exile to Formenos, leaving behind Indis and his other children. Fëanor's wife Nerdanel also declined to go into exile, instead remaining in Tirion to dwell with Indis.
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), Morgoth's Ring, "Part Three. The Later Quenta Silmarillion: (II) The Second Phase: Later versions of the Story of Finwë and Míriel", pp. 278-9
claims.section: section == History == > Unrest of the Noldor

claims.text: The Later Quenta second phase material names a fifth child of Finwë and Indis, Faniel, who is not included in the list of Indis' children in the Shibboleth or The Silmarillion. Two positions in the birth order are attested for Faniel: in Laws and Customs and the second draft of Finwë and Míriel, Faniel is the third child and Írimë is the fifth child. In the fourth and final revision of Finwë and Míriel, Faniel is the fifth child and Írimë (here named "Finvain") is the third.
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), Morgoth's Ring, "Part Three. The Later Quenta Silmarillion: (II) The Second Phase: Laws and Customs among the Eldar, [Text A]", pp. 238-9; J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), Morgoth's Ring, "Part Three. The Later Quenta Silmarillion: (II) The Second Phase: Later versions of the Story of Finwë and Míriel", Note 10, p. 265; J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), Morgoth's Ring, "Part Three. The Later Quenta Silmarillion: (II) The Second Phase: Later versions of the Story of Finwë and Míriel", author's footnote, p. 262
claims.section: section == Other versions of the legendarium == > Fifth child

claims.text: The name "Indis" first appears in The Annals of Aman (c. 1950-1) in reference to the only wife of Finwë. When Tolkien first revisited the Quenta Silmarillion c. 1951, he discarded the name "Indis" entirely, with the wife of Finwë being named "Míriel."
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), Morgoth's Ring, "Part Two. The Annals of Aman: Notes [on Section 3]", Notes 3 and 5, p. 87}}; J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), Morgoth's Ring, "Part Three. The Later Quenta Silmarillion: (I) The First Phase: 6. Of the Silmarils and the Darkening of Valinor", §46b, p. 185}}
claims.section: section == Other versions of the legendarium == > Other uses of the name "Indis"

claims.text: Following the publication of The Lord of the Rings, Tolkien returned to the matter of the First Age and began the work of "remoulding" the existing texts with a view towards publication. This began with The Earliest Version of the Story of Finwë and Míriel (c. 1958). In this tale, the name "Indis" was given to a new character, "Indis of the Vanyar," the second wife of Finwë. This Indis would also appear in the essay Laws and Customs among the Eldar and subsequent revisions to Finwë and Míriel that were developed in connection with the "second phase" drafts of the Later Quenta Silmarillion (all c. 1958). References to this new Indis were also inserted into the text of The Annals of Aman during this period.
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), Morgoth's Ring, "Part Three. The Later Quenta Silmarillion: (II) The Second Phase: Of the Thieves' Quarrel": Commentary, Note on Dating, p. 300; J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), Morgoth's Ring, "Part Three. The Later Quenta Silmarillion: (II) The Second Phase: The Earliest Version of the Story of Finwë and Míriel", p. 207; J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), Morgoth's Ring, "Part Three. The Later Quenta Silmarillion: (II) The Second Phase: Laws and Customs among the Eldar", p.237; J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), Morgoth's Ring, "Part Three. The Later Quenta Silmarillion: (II) The Second Phase: Later versions of the Story of Finwë and Míriel", §23-27 pp. 261-2; J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), Morgoth's Ring, "Part Two. The Annals of Aman: Notes [on Section 4]", Notes 4, p. 101}}
claims.section: section == Other versions of the legendarium == > Other uses of the name "Indis"

claims.text: In the first scheme, Indis was born at Cuiviénen to Ingwë and his wife Ilwen before Oromë discovered the Elves. In this scheme she also had an older brother, Ingwil, as well as an unnamed younger sibling.
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, Carl F. Hostetter (ed.), "Part One. Time and Ageing: XVII. Generational Schemes", The Nature of Middle-earth, HarperCollins, 2021, pp. 127-8
claims.section: section == Other versions of the legendarium == > Relation to Ingwë > Daughter of Ingwë

claims.text: In the second scheme, she was likewise born at Cuiviénen before the Elves were discovered by Oromë. However, in this scheme her mother is not mentioned, and she was the eldest child of Ingwë with her younger sibling being born just before the start of the Great March.
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, Carl F. Hostetter (ed.), "Part One. Time and Ageing: XVII. Generational Schemes", The Nature of Middle-earth, HarperCollins, 2021, p. 142
claims.section: section == Other versions of the legendarium == > Relation to Ingwë > Daughter of Ingwë

claims.text: An entry in the Words, Phrases and Passages (c. late '50s) published in Parma Eldalamberon 17 also identifies Fingolfin's mother as "the daughter of Ingwi." Elsewhere in that text, "Ingwi" is defined as the "people of Ingwë".
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, "Words, Phrases and Passages in Various Tongues in The Lord of the Rings", in Parma Eldalamberon XVII (edited by Christopher Gilson), p. 39; J.R.R. Tolkien, "Words, Phrases and Passages in Various Tongues in The Lord of the Rings", in Parma Eldalamberon XVII (edited by Christopher Gilson), p. 154
claims.section: section == Other versions of the legendarium == > Relation to Ingwë > Daughter of Ingwë

claims.text: Tolkien revisited the subject of Indis' parentage for the last time in the essay The Shibboleth of Fëanor (c. 1968), in which Indis is identified as "Indis of the House of Ingwë." In a contemporary excursus, The names of Finwë's descendants, published in The Peoples of Middle-earth as an appendix to the Shibboleth, Tolkien stated that Indis "is said to have been the daughter of King Ingwë's sister.
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), The Peoples of Middle-earth, "XI. The Shibboleth of Fëanor", "The case of the Quenya change of Þ to s", p. 334; J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), The Peoples of Middle-earth, "XI. The Shibboleth of Fëanor", "The names of Finwë's descendants", p. 343
claims.section: section == Other versions of the legendarium == > Relation to Ingwë > Niece of Ingwë

claims.text: In a note on the above excursus, Tolkien stated that in the person of Eldarion "the lines of all the Three Kings of the High Elves (Eldar), Ingwë, Finwë, and Olwë and Elwë were united and alone preserved in Middle-earth." In an editorial comment on this note, Christopher Tolkien noted the apparent absence of direct descent from Ingwë to Eldarion, stating "It is hard to know what my father had in mind when he wrote the opening of this note."
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), The Peoples of Middle-earth, "XI. The Shibboleth of Fëanor", "Notes", Note 53, pp. 364-5
claims.section: section == Other versions of the legendarium == > Relation to Ingwë > Unspecified descendant of Ingwë

claims.text: The name Indor is in Gnomish, most likely being the word indor ("master of house, lord") used as a personal name. Its Qenya cognate is also Indor.
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), The Book of Lost Tales Part Two, "Appendix: Names in the Lost Tales - Part II", entry Indor, p. 343; J.R.R. Wynne, and Bill Welden), "Official Name List", p. 103

claims.text: In the later legendarium, according to The Children of Húrin, Indor was the name of Aerin's father.
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), The Children of Húrin, "The Return of Túrin to Dor-lómin", p. 189
claims.section: section == Other versions of the legendarium ==

claims.text: Ingoldo, or i·Ñoldo, was the mothername of both Finarfin and his son Finrod Felagund. It became a frequently given name in Númenor; in the Third Age in Gondor, it was shortened to Ingold under influence of Westron.
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), The Peoples of Middle-earth, "XI. The Shibboleth of Fëanor", "Notes", p. 360, note 30

claims.text: At the time of the War of the Ring, Ingold was the leader of a guard of Gondorian soldiers posted at the Forannest, the northern gate of Rammas Echor, the encircling wall of Pelennor Fields. They were repairing the wall on 8 March, when Gandalf and Pippin with Ingold’s permission passed into the townlands of Minas Tirith on their journey from Rohan to the city of Gondor.
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, The Lord of the Rings, The Return of the King, "Minas Tirith"

claims.text: Less than five days after Gandalf had passed through, an army from the East had crossed the River Anduin and broke the Rammas. Ingold’s guard was the last to escape from the host, reporting to Minas Tirith that the northward road had been taken by the enemy. Due to Ingold’s news, it was thought that the Rohirrim could not come to Gondor’s aid.
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, The Lord of the Rings, The Return of the King, "The Siege of Gondor"

claims.text: Ingwë is described as being tall and beautiful, and his hair as golden and curly. He is also said to have been "more given to thought than arts".
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, Carl F. Hostetter (ed.), "Part One. Time and Ageing: XVII. Generational Schemes", The Nature of Middle-earth, HarperCollins, 2021, pp. 127-128; J.R.R. Tolkien, Carl F. Hostetter (ed.), "Part Two. Body, Mind and Spirit: IV. Hair", The Nature of Middle-earth, HarperCollins, 2021, p. 186

claims.text:
The name Ingwë is in Quenya. It means "chief", being derived from the root ING ("highest", "top"), to which is attached the suffix -wë ("person").
The Vanyar called themselves the Ingwer, the chieftains, on account of being considered the leaders and principal kindred of the Eldar, and their king's proper title was Ingwë Ingweron: ‘chief of the chieftains’.
In the earlier Etymologies, Ingwë is said to be a compound of ing ("first") + the ending -we ("man").
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), The Peoples of Middle-earth, "XI. The Shibboleth of Fëanor", "The names of Finwë's descendants", p. 340; J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), The Lost Road and Other Writings, Part Three: "The Etymologies", entries"ING", "WEG"
